01-reality-of-ownership.title: The reality of ownership
01-reality-of-ownership.standfirst: What the first three years of yacht ownership actually look like, in time and in money. The folkloric numbers do not survive contact with the data.
paragraphs: In 2025 the estimated value of sales of yachts over 24 metres reached USD 8.5 billion, a 70 percent rise on the year before and exceeded in the past decade only by the post-Covid peak of 2021. The estimate is BOAT International’s, based on asking prices, as published in Knight Frank’s Wealth Report 2026. Knight Frank names US demand as the biggest catalyst, with US buyers rushing to close before the year end once the One Big Beautiful Bill Act reintroduced a 100 percent depreciation bonus. The market grew largely on US demand and a change in the tax code; the demand structure underneath did not.

paragraphs.text: The folklore of the 10 percent rule

paragraphs: The industry shorthand for annual operating cost is 10 percent of the yacht’s purchase price per year, quoted by brokers and management companies alike. The rule has no traceable origin. It survives because it is roughly correct for new, mid-sized, lightly used yachts, and because it is easy.
It is also wrong for most readers of The First Owner’s Reference.

YachtBuyer calls the rule “at best, obsolete or even misleading” for older or larger crewed vessels. As the asset depreciates, the percentage rises mechanically: running cost is a function of size and complexity, not residual value. A 50m yacht worth EUR 30 million eight years after a EUR 50 million build does not become 40 percent cheaper to operate; the EUR 5 million annual run rate that was 10 percent of value at purchase is now nearly 17 percent.

Working ranges from independent practitioner sources (Fraser Yachts, Ocean Independence, Foreland Marine) cluster between 8 and 15 percent for the first decade. For yachts over 40 metres, or older than seven years, the figure is closer to 12 to 20 percent. Charter-active vessels run higher still.

Budget 12 to 15 percent for a typical 40m to 50m new build operated privately at moderate use, and revise upward for charter operation, larger size, or older age. Do not let any party paid contingent on a deal closing tell you otherwise.

paragraphs.text: What you actually buy

paragraphs: The cost categories do not rank the way most buyers expect. Crew, not fuel, is the dominant line.

Crew accounts for 30 to 40 percent of annual operating cost and rises with size. A captain on a 50m yacht costs EUR 10,000 to 16,000 per month per the YPI Crew 2026 salary guide; on an 80m, EUR 16,000 to 23,000. Quay Crew’s 2025/26 captain survey records a 7 percent rise in the 70 to 79m bracket since its previous survey in 2023, and 63 percent of the 367 captains surveyed on time-for-time rotation.

Maintenance and repair, 14 to 18 percent. Insurance, 10 to 14 percent. Berths and marina fees, 8 to 12 percent. Fuel, 8 to 12 percent, higher on charter-active hulls. Management fees, 3 to 5 percent. Regulatory and class compliance, 2 to 3 percent. Contingency, 6 to 10 percent. The remainder is provisioning, communications, owner travel, and the lines that simply happen.

A 40m motor yacht at moderate use (400 cruising hours per year, diesel assumed at EUR 1.30 to 1.80 per litre, a working range: marina prices, duty-free supply to commercially registered yachts and 2026 price movements all vary) runs EUR 130,000 to 250,000 per year on fuel alone. A 50m motor yacht on the same hours burns EUR 200,000 to 350,000, the figure chapter 8 compares with a sailing yacht of the same length.
Practitioner estimates place typical use at 4 to 8 weeks a year; committed users reach 12 to 16. What those weeks buy is a fixed cost that runs whether the yacht is used or not.

The Superyacht Report OpEx Survey, Q2 2026, answered by captains in the 28 to 83 metre fleet, corroborates the working ranges from a separate base. 62 percent of yachts in that band report annual operating budgets above EUR / USD 2 million; 31 percent sit in the 4 to 6 million band, and 8 percent above 6 million. On private programmes in that sample, owners are aboard an average of 17 weeks a year, while the yacht, the crew and the costs run for all 52. The difference from the 4 to 8 weeks above lies in the samples: one is a practitioner estimate for typical owners, the other a captain-reported survey of larger yachts in active private use. Up to 24 weeks of the year can be spent in yard for maintenance or refit, and an operating estimate should say whether that time is included. Crew wages alone can reach EUR / USD 100,000 per month when owner and guests are aboard, and run year-round regardless.

paragraphs.text: The depreciation reality

paragraphs: Broker-published figures agree on the shape of the curve more than on its numbers. Yatco puts the first-year loss at 10 to 15 percent, then about 5 percent a year, about 30 percent by year five. IYC puts the first-year correction at 10 to 20 percent, with most yachts “reaching 40-50% of their original price in five years”, read here as a five-year loss of 40 to 50 percent. Together they put the typical loss at year five at about 30 to 50 percent of the purchase price, after which the curve flattens. Yacht Hunter’s Chris Mortimer rejects fixed schedules altogether: value, he argues, follows condition, market and comparable sales.

Quality builders hold value much better. Feadship, Lürssen, Royal Huisman, Vitters, and Baltic Yachts hulls can lose only single-digit percentages annually after year five. There is no peer-reviewed academic study of yacht depreciation; all published curves are broker-aggregated and self-reported, and should be read as indicative.

A yacht is not an investment. In the first year it typically loses about as much value as it costs to run. A USD 30 million yacht held for five years at moderate use will typically have lost USD 9 to 13 million in value and consumed another USD 15 to 22 million in operating cost.

paragraphs.text: The charter delusion

paragraphs: Charter is often presented to first-time owners as a way to offset the cost of ownership. For the median yacht, the published arithmetic does not bear that out.

BOAT International’s published case studies (April 2025) are the cleanest public evidence. A 48m motor yacht at EUR 250,000 to 310,000 per week, 7 charter weeks per year, generated EUR 1,592,000 in net income against EUR 1,575,000 in running cost: effectively break-even, before the owner’s own use. A 47m sailing yacht at 9 weeks made a EUR 444,000 loss; an 85m motor at 8 weeks lost EUR 430,000. The exception is a 60m concept, Hill Robinson’s “Perfect Charter Yacht” launched at the 2024 Monaco Yacht Show, modelled at 12 charter weeks for a net revenue target of EUR 2 million. It is a design study rather than a trading yacht, and its figures assume premium rates and high-season weeks given to charter.

Most charter operations subsidise rather than recover ownership cost. The growth of the global charter market (Precedence Research: USD 8.39 billion in 2024, forecast USD 16.92 billion by 2033) is driven by charter demand, not by owners profiting from it.
Charter can pay for a small minority of well-run programmes. A first yacht rarely has those conditions in place from the start.

paragraphs.text: The case for ownership

paragraphs: None of this argues against ownership. It argues against buying on the strength of a quoted budget that nobody has tested. Made with the full cost in view, the right ownership decision is one of the great purchases a person can make. Taken on folkloric numbers and contingent advice, it is among the more costly errors an ultra-high-net-worth (UHNW) buyer can make.

Ownership makes sense when the owner intends to use the yacht for at least 12 weeks per year, plans to hold for at least seven years, has the cash flow to absorb operating cost without strain, and wants a programme charter cannot deliver. What the owner gets is repeated, predictable, family-led use of a known yacht, specified, crewed and operated to his or her own preferences. The case for ownership is operational rather than financial.

The book’s own case files show what that looks like in practice. In the chapter 1 case, the owner’s second yacht, a 46m semi-custom, was bought with a team he paid directly at known rates, about USD 320,000 on a USD 24 million acquisition. In year five the captain hired through an independent recruitment process at the start is still aboard, the crew has stayed largely intact, and operating cost has run at 13 to 14 percent of original capex a year, inside the band set out before he bought.

Continuity of that kind depends on the owner as well as the crew. Asked what most often drives turnover, Erica Lay, founder and director of EL Crew Co, answered “Inconsistency from the top”, which she says “can come from the owner, the captain, or the management structure”. In her words: “Crew can handle hard work. They can handle long hours and demanding programmes. What they struggle with is unpredictability and a lack of trust in leadership.” Ella Johnson, captain of a 34m Baltic Yachts performance sloop, says the yacht “looks the same seven years on”, and credits “both the yard’s design and build and the crew over the years who have looked after her.”

Ownership also costs time. In the chapter 9 case, the adviser estimated that a 49m yacht would take 40 to 60 days a year of the owner’s direct attention, through season planning, refit scheduling, supplier conversations and crew matters, on top of 80 to 120 days of family use. That buyer decided he did not want the commitment and did not proceed. For an owner who does want it, those days are part of the price, and they belong in the plan alongside the money.

Ask whether your intended use pattern fits. The running cost calculator on this site tests your own numbers against data from the Mediterranean Yacht Brokers Association (MYBA), Pantaenius, Quay Crew, IGY and aggregated practitioner sources.

If, after that exercise, the answer is still ownership, the rest of The First Owner’s Reference is written for that reader. The remaining chapters cover the market, how the industry works, the acquisition process, new build versus brokerage, refit, operations, and how to build the team that protects the buyer. Read in any order, applying the independence test in chapter 9 to anyone proposing to advise.

02-reading-the-market.title: Reading the market
02-reading-the-market.standfirst: The number of people worth more than USD 30 million has grown by nearly 30 percent in five years. The order book contracted for the second consecutive year. The market is becoming harder to buy correctly, not easier.
paragraphs: Two facts about the market going into 2027 are seldom stated alongside one another. The number of people worth more than USD 30 million has grown by nearly 30 percent in five years (Knight Frank), while the order book for yachts above 24 metres contracted for the second consecutive year. The number of potential buyers is rising sharply; the number of new yachts being contracted is falling, and build slots at the established yards are scarce.

Trade press often describes the moment as a boom. The figures below describe something narrower: fewer new-build contracts against a growing number of potential buyers, scarce slots at the established yards, and a brokerage market in which well-priced yachts sell and over-priced ones wait.

paragraphs.text: The wealth side

paragraphs: The Knight Frank Wealth Sizing Model, 20th edition for 2026, places the global UHNWI population (net wealth above USD 30 million) at 713,626, up from 551,435 in 2021. The five-year change is 162,191 new UHNWIs, equivalent to 89 individuals crossing the USD 30 million threshold every day for five years.

41 percent of new UHNWIs were created in the United States, and the country’s share of the global UHNW population is forecast to reach 41 percent by 2031, up from 33 percent in 2021; the concentration is still intensifying. Saudi Arabia leads billionaire growth at a forecast 183 percent over five years, Indonesia leads UHNWI growth at 82 percent, and India is forecast to add UHNWIs faster in absolute terms than any other economy. BOAT International identifies the rise of Indian wealth as one of the industry’s next big demand engines and reports that wealthy Indian entrepreneurs are translating it into yacht ownership primarily in the Mediterranean, with some choosing Dubai or Abu Dhabi as a secondary base (Knight Frank Wealth Report 2026).

The Capgemini World Wealth Report 2025 adds the inheritance figures: USD 83.5 trillion of wealth will be inherited by Gen X, millennials, and Gen Z by 2048. 81 percent of next-generation HNWIs intend to switch from their parents’ wealth management firm within one to two years of inheritance. Many readers of The First Owner’s Reference will therefore be one of two kinds of buyer: a principal who has recently sold a business, or an heir reviewing the advisers their parents used.

paragraphs.text: The yacht side

paragraphs: The 2026 BOAT International Global Order Book records 1,093 yachts of 24m and above on order or in build, down from 1,138 in the 2025 edition and the second consecutive annual decline by unit count. Average length has risen to 40.8m and average tonnage to 551 GT, up from 40.0m and 507 GT in the 2025 edition; unit count peaked in the 2023 to 2024 window and has eased, so a claim that the order book is at a peak holds only for length and tonnage. New contracts are falling with it: Northrop & Johnson counts 216 new-build sales of 24m and above from January to September 2026, against 266 in the same months of 2025 and 397 in 2022. The 2026 figure is provisional, since late-reported sales are still being added (Northrop & Johnson, Q3 2026 Superyacht Market Report).

The breakdown by hull type from BoatPro: 837 motor, 101 explorer, 69 sailing, 63 open, 23 sportfish. Explorer has consolidated as the second-largest single category at roughly nine percent of the order book (101 of 1,093).

Italy now dominates production: 568 units, 52 percent of the order book. Azimut Benetti is ranked first for the 26th consecutive year (5,924 metres across 163 yachts), Sanlorenzo with Nautor Swan second. The Netherlands is second by tonnage (107,796 GT across 66 units), reflecting larger average length. Turkey is third (82,383 GT across 141). Germany is fourth (78,651 GT across just 18, output concentrated at the very top).

Top-tier yards are sold out. Lürssen’s large-yacht capacity is committed several years ahead, enlarged by its 2025 acquisition of the insolvent Nobiskrug yard at Rendsburg. Feadship slot availability was reported in trade press in 2026 as extending to 2028 to 2029, with Project Solent due for delivery in summer 2027. Oceanco delivered the 111m DreAMBoat in November 2025, 45 months after contract and, on the yard’s figures, about 18 months faster than a conventional custom build of that size: the counter-example of speed at the top. Heesen runs a speculative-build model, with hulls in build for delivery between 2026 and 2028. The constraint extends to the mid-tier: Damen Yachting’s Yacht Support range is booked through Q4 2028 / Q1 2029 on certain models, and Sanlorenzo’s order book extends to the same window on the SX, SD, and Steel ranges. On the sailing yacht side, Southern Wind reported in May 2026 that its next available build slot is in 2028 (Superyacht Investor); Sanlorenzo’s UK and Ireland office reports late-Q1 2026 buyer-meeting volume approximately 10 percent above the same window in 2025.

For a first-time buyer entering in 2027, the main decision comes before the choice of yard: whether to take a brokerage yacht now, take a slot at a mid-tier yard with capacity, or wait three to four years for a delivery slot at a top-tier German or Dutch builder. Each path carries a different cost, risk and timescale, and chapter 5 compares them.

paragraphs.text: The order book tracker on this site holds the 2026 Global Order Book figures by yard, country, and hull type, with the sources named on every line.
Brokerage in 2025 and 2026

paragraphs: By Edmiston’s measure, brokerage sales of yachts over 30 metres, 2025 was the strongest year on record. Its 2025 review records more than EUR 7.1 billion across 363 sales, 15 percent more sales than in 2024. Yachts asking more than EUR 40 million were 7 percent of sales by number and 52 percent of value. Other published totals measure different things, including the USD 8.5 billion cited in chapter 1, BOAT International’s estimate of 2025 sales of yachts over 24 metres based on asking prices (Knight Frank Wealth Report 2026). Edmiston reports selling more yachts over 40 metres, and more over EUR 20 million, than any other brokerage.

Days on market is the clearest published test of whether a yacht is priced to sell: a buyer should read any listing’s time on market and price-reduction history against the most recent published median for its size band, and note the date of that median. The latest figures for yachts of 24m and above are Northrop & Johnson’s, for the third quarter of 2026. Yachts sold in that quarter had been listed for an average of 445 days, against 542 in the second quarter. Asking prices were cut 1,949 times between January and September, up 7.2 percent on the same months of 2025, and yachts cut in the third quarter had been on the market for a median of 386 days. Neither figure is a size-band median, and a cut asking price is not the final discount. Shorter selling times alongside more frequent price cuts suggest a market dividing on price: yachts priced close to what buyers will pay sell, and the rest wait and are cut.

Anders Kurtén, CEO of Fraser, gave a benchmark in early 2026: a normalised year would typically produce around 50 brokerage transactions above 30 metres for the house, with January 2026 alone running at twelve yachts in twelve days (Superyacht Investor, March 2026). The pace is consistent with the shorter selling times above.

Asking prices have eased slightly from their 2021 to 2023 highs (YATCO). The 70 metre and above segment hit record values in 2025: Knight Frank’s Wealth Report 2026 records sales in the bracket up 60 percent year on year, with the 119m Feadship Breakthrough sale the largest single transaction. The average asking price of a sold yacht across the over-24 metre fleet was US$16.6 million in 2025 (Knight Frank, citing BOAT International), and 2025 saw the highest number of new yachts entering the brokerage market in seven years; through mid-February 2026, 58 sales had generated US$647 million, up 34.6 percent year on year (BOAT International data, in the same report).

The first nine months of 2026 were level by count and lower by value. Northrop & Johnson records 472 sales of yachts of 24m and above, against 477 in the same months of 2025, worth USD 5.2 billion against USD 5.46 billion. Yachts aged nine years or less made up 197 of those sales, about 42 percent. The heaviest asking-price cuts fell on yachts aged 25 to 29 years, at 31.1 percent on average. The count reaches down to 24m, so it does not compare with the Edmiston figure above (Northrop & Johnson, Q3 2026 Superyacht Market Report).

paragraphs.text: The geographic shift

paragraphs: Three claims about geographic shift recur in trade press. The data supports the first, partly supports the second and does not support the third.

United States dominance is supported. BOAT International puts US share of yacht transactions at 45 to 50 percent in 2025, the highest on record, partly driven by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act 100 percent depreciation provision.

The tariff side of the same trade environment has changed three times since April 2025. BoatPro’s tariff brief, drawn from The Washington Post and Forbes, documents the April 2025 tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), which raised effective US tariff rates on imported yachts: China 20 to 40 percent, Turkey 10 to 25, Taiwan 10 to 20, Italy 2.2 to 15, Germany 1.4 to 15, France 1.2 to 15, Netherlands 0.7 to 15, UK 0.97 to 10. On 20 February 2026 the Supreme Court held that IEEPA does not authorise tariffs, and on 4 March the Court of International Trade ordered the duties refunded to all importers of record. A temporary 10 percent tariff under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 applied from 24 February to 24 July 2026. Since 24 July Section 301 duties of 10 or 12.5 percent have applied to goods from 60 economies. For goods from the European Union the Section 301 duty tops the ordinary (MFN) duty up to a combined 10 percent, and nothing is added where the MFN duty is already 10 percent or more; UK goods carry a flat 10 percent (USTR notice of action, 23 July 2026). A US buyer ordering from a European yard should confirm the rate that applies at contract and delivery, and the contract should say who bears any change. In 2025 some buyers responded by acquiring duty-paid hulls from US dealer inventory rather than ordering direct.

The claim of a European collapse is partly supported. Europe’s share of sales transactions fell to 52 percent in the first half of 2025, from 60 percent a year earlier (IYC mid-year report, July 2025). Western Mediterranean sales more than doubled, from 11 in the first quarter of 2024 to 27 in the first quarter of 2025 (Denison Yacht Sales, Q1 2025 market report). The European market remains the second largest by a wide margin.

The claim of an Asian retreat is not supported by fleet data. SuperYacht Times counts the active Asia-Pacific fleet over 30m at 445 in 2023, 530 in 2024 and 586 in 2025, of which 350 were owned by Asian nationals (Asia-Pacific Superyacht Report 2026, as summarised by ICOMIA). The claim appears to rest on new-build orders rather than the operating fleet.
The claim of a Russian collapse is also overstated. SuperYacht Times iQ data shows Russian ownership share moving from 9.1 percent in 2022 to 8.1 percent in 2023, a decline rather than a collapse.

paragraphs.text: What this means for a buyer

paragraphs: First, the wealth pool is increasingly American: 41 percent of new UHNWIs were created in the United States, and the US share is forecast to reach 41 percent by 2031. It also includes a growing number of heirs, 81 percent of whom intend to change wealth manager within two years of inheriting. The demographic shift is now visible on the show floor: Southern Wind reports the new owner of the SW108 Kalantis is in his 30s, with average ownership age across three Southern Wind hulls at Palma May 2026 in the late 40s (Superyacht Investor). VistaJet’s Q1 2026 data corroborates from the aviation side: 47 percent of first-time flyers in the quarter were under 45, a record high. These are small samples, but they point to first-time buyers younger than is often assumed.

Second, supply is concentrated at Italian volume yards (Azimut Benetti, Sanlorenzo) for unit count and Northern European custom yards (Lürssen, Feadship, Oceanco) for prestige and value retention. The prestige tier is sold out for several years. A first-time buyer cannot have a 50m Lürssen within a year of deciding.

Third, the information a buyer needs to judge an asking price is published. Listing portals show each yacht’s time on market and its price cuts, and Northrop & Johnson’s quarterly figures give a benchmark to read them against. A yacht listed well beyond the average for yachts that sold, with a record of cuts, is evidence that its asking price is above what buyers will pay.
The figures in this chapter describe price and supply, not motive. Robb Maass of Alley, Maass, Rogers & Lindsay, speaking on a panel in March 2026:

paragraphs.text: It’s not money that drives buying and building yachts. What determines whether someone builds or buys a yacht is psychological.
paragraphs.attribution: Robb Maass, Alley, Maass, Rogers & Lindsay, March 2026 (Superyacht Investor)

paragraphs: Whatever the motive, the price paid can be tested against the published record: the yacht’s time on market and price cuts, recent comparable sales and, for new build, the yard’s actual delivery slot. That record is now detailed enough for a buyer and their adviser to question a broker’s view of price on the evidence.

03-how-the-industry-works.title: How the industry actually works
03-how-the-industry-works.standfirst: In most superyacht purchases, the broker guiding the buyer is paid out of the seller’s commission, and the suppliers that broker introduces may pay the broker again. Neither payment appears on the buyer’s invoices.
paragraphs: The first thing a new owner often learns, months after the first contract is signed, is who was paying the people around the acquisition. The broker who walked them around shipyards in Viareggio and Vlissingen, introduced the captain candidates, and recommended the law firm, the surveyor, and the management company was paid by the seller. In some transactions, the same broker represented the seller. The questions that would have raised this are not in the standard first-time buyer’s kit.

This follows from how the market pays its people more than from the conduct of any one broker. The alternative, where the buyer pays their own adviser at the rates such advice costs, feels expensive at the moment of the decision and cheap years later, looking back from a second yacht.

paragraphs.text: The two parallel commission norms

paragraphs: A brokerage sale of a 40-metre yacht for EUR 28 million carries between about EUR 1.7 million and EUR 2.8 million in commission, depending on which of two parallel norms is applied. Both are presented as “the standard” by the brokers using them, although they are not the same.

The US norm, associated with the International Yacht Brokers Association (IYBA), is a flat 10 percent of gross sale price, paid by the seller. On a USD 50 million sale, that is USD 5 million. The Mediterranean Yacht Brokers Association (MYBA) sliding scale is 10 percent on the first 10 million, 5 percent on the second, 2.5 percent above; published descriptions give the bands in US dollars. On a USD 50 million sale, that is USD 2.25 million. Applied in euros, the bands give EUR 1.7 million on the EUR 28 million sale above, and the commission agreement should state the currency of the bands. The seller does not always know which is being applied. The buyer is rarely told. The buyer’s broker is paid out of the seller’s commission, typically half of it or a little less. On the US base that is 4 to 5 percent of the gross sale price. On the MYBA scale it is smaller: about EUR 850,000, or 3 percent, on the EUR 28 million sale.

Practitioner commentary attributed to Cromwell Littlejohn (Northrop & Johnson) at industry events acknowledges that brokers can be reluctant to publish reduced commission rates on the central-agency listing, on the basis that disclosure may suppress buyer-broker viewings. The system, on his published reading, can reward opacity. Offered here as practitioner opinion; Northrop & Johnson itself states a commitment to full transparency.

paragraphs.text: Dual agency and the IYBA standard form

paragraphs: The IYBA Purchase and Sale Agreement, the standard contract used in most US-jurisdiction yacht transactions, contains a dual-agency clause that constitutes pre-emptive consent. Signing the standard form means the buyer and seller have already agreed that the broker may act for both sides, with carve-outs (the broker cannot tell the seller the buyer’s maximum, cannot tell the buyer the seller’s minimum). A broker bound by those carve-outs cannot act fully for either side, and the standard form makes that the starting position of the transaction.

Ya Mon Expeditions LLC v. IYBA et al. is a Sherman Act class action in the US District Court for the Southern District of Florida alleging conspiracy to fix commissions across the industry. In January 2025 Judge K. Michael Moore dismissed the complaint without prejudice and with leave to amend. That order was later vacated and the case stayed while one defendant, YATCO, appealed the refusal to send the claims to arbitration; the Eleventh Circuit affirmed that refusal on 10 June 2026, and the case has since resumed in the district court. The pleadings document a transaction in which both sides of a sale were brokered by the same firm, with the firm collecting both sides of the 10 percent commission. No court has ruled on the merits. The litigation shows that the practice is questioned seriously enough to reach federal court.

California requires explicit dual-agency disclosure. Florida operates under transactional-brokerage rules where full agency duties to either side are diluted by default. The UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) does not regulate yacht sales because they are not a regulated financial instrument; the Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) does not regulate brokerage commissions. Beyond state rules of this kind in the United States, no major jurisdiction has a financial regulator that supervises yacht brokerage conduct. From 10 July 2027 the EU Anti-Money Laundering Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/1624) brings traders in high-value watercraft within the anti-money-laundering regime. They must carry out customer due diligence, and under Article 74 they must report to the national financial intelligence unit every sale of a watercraft for non-commercial use at a price of EUR 7.5 million or more. That is supervision of who the buyer is and where the money comes from, not of how the broker is paid or whom the broker represents.

paragraphs.text: Camper & Nicholsons and Fincantieri

paragraphs: Camper & Nicholsons was acquired in 2014 by Coliseum Services SA, a Geneva-based vehicle subsequently renamed the 1782 Group. In May 2015, the Italian state-controlled shipbuilder Fincantieri acquired a minority stake via a capital increase, with Coliseum Services remaining the majority shareholder. Lai Sun Development Company Limited, the Hong Kong-listed conglomerate, bought 50 percent in October 2016, and in February 2017 Fincantieri raised its holding to the other 50 percent as the 1782 Group left the shareholding. By May 2026 a Lai Sun subsidiary held 98.27 percent of Camper & Nicholsons International S.A. (Lai Sun’s announcement to the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, 28 May 2026).

For several years, then, C&N had on its capitalisation table an Italian shipbuilder that builds yachts C&N sells. A conflict of that kind lasts as long as the shareholding does, and a buyer offered a yacht through any brokerage can ask, in writing, whether a builder holds shares in it.

On 28 May 2026, Lai Sun signed to sell an initial 80 percent interest in C&N International to Wave Expandary Limited, for EUR 40 million on a valuation of EUR 50 million for the whole company. That is roughly twelve times FY2025 EBITDA on management figures, against C&N revenue of HK$270.7 million and net profit after tax of HK$13.1 million. Wave Expandary is guaranteed by Sea Expandary Limited, the vertically integrated yacht-industry platform announced in February 2026 by JD.com founder Richard Liu Qiangdong. Sea Expandary’s stated USD 700 million commitment runs across R&D, manufacturing, brokerage, and after-sales, focused on new-energy propulsion and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. Put and call options govern the remaining interest from 31 December 2027, each estimated at EUR 9.135 million. Completion was subject to regulatory and shareholder approvals, with a long stop of 30 September 2026. In October 2026 C&N announced that Benjamin Bensahel, previously its chief commercial officer for Europe and the Middle East, had succeeded Paolo Casani as CEO following Sea Expandary’s acquisition of a majority stake. The announcement shows no Fincantieri holding: before the sale, the Lai Sun group held 98.27 percent of C&N International.

C&N’s new controlling shareholder operates its own yacht-manufacturing platform alongside the brokerage. The disclosure question the Fincantieri arrangement raised returns in the same form, against a larger and more recent counterparty: is the buyer told when C&N markets a Sea Expandary hull?

The Fincantieri example is the cleanest, but not the only one. In November 2025 the US private equity firm Ancient (Alexander Klabin) acquired a strategic stake in Burgess, the firm’s first outside investor in 50 years. Fraser and Northrop & Johnson were acquired by the listed US dealer MarineMax in 2019 and 2020. In August 2026 MarineMax agreed to be sold to Safe Harbor Marinas, owned by Blackstone Infrastructure, for USD 1.5 billion, with completion expected by the end of 2026; both brokerages would then sit in the same group as a global marina operator that also owns the Rybovich refit yard in West Palm Beach (chapter 6). Denison Yachting was sold by the Denison family to OneWater Marine (NASDAQ: ONEW) in April 2022, and in September 2026 OneWater agreed to sell a majority interest to OceanWorld Group while keeping a minority investment.

Several of the largest brokerage names have taken outside capital since 2019. Private equity owners look for EBITDA growth, which rewards selling more services per yacht, capturing recurring management and refit spend, and consolidating commission pools. On that reading, the “free advice” model becomes more valuable to such owners, not less.

paragraphs.text: Retrocession economics

paragraphs: Referral fees from yacht-management firms, refit yards, paint contractors, electronics integrators, insurance brokers, finance providers, crew agencies, and class societies to the introducing broker are an open secret. OnboardOnline’s legal column states the rule plainly: referral fees are legal only if disclosed, must be reflected in the closing statement to seller and buyer, and undisclosed payments to a captain are potentially criminal. No equivalent rule compels the brokerage house to disclose retrocessions on ongoing services to its yacht-owning client.

On a EUR 4 million repaint, a 5 percent retrocession is EUR 200,000. On a yacht whose management company runs an annual operating budget of EUR 5 million, a 10 percent introductory retrocession calculated on that budget is EUR 500,000 in year one. Neither appears on any invoice to the owner, because the broker is not invoicing the owner; the owner pays the yard, the management company, and the paint contractor, and the retrocessions flow inside the supplier’s books.

Retrocessions are widely acknowledged in the trade, but they are paid privately and the published record does not show which firms take them, so no firm is named in this section. When the buyer’s adviser earns more because the buyer spends more with counterparties the adviser has steered them toward, the adviser’s interests and the buyer’s pull apart. Disclosed in writing, that payment is something the buyer can weigh. Undisclosed, it is a cost the buyer carries without knowing whose interest it served.
The same observation appears in Hein Velema’s published comment on new build broker arrangements, May 2026:

paragraphs.text: In a new build, the broker often represents the owner in the deal, but the broker is being paid by the shipyard. That is a mismatch. Owners generally know that a broker works on commission. They do not always know how much, or on what.
paragraphs.attribution: Hein Velema, Secretary General, Superyacht Alliance for Professional Standards, May 2026

paragraphs: An experienced broker, well led and open about how they are paid, noticeably reduces execution risk on a transaction the buyer would not otherwise close cleanly. They walk inventory the buyer has not had the time to walk, read paint and machinery and pricing patterns from the inside, and know which sellers are negotiating and which are window-shopping. Owners are by construction hard to reach; the broker who carries that relationship has earned it.

paragraphs.text: If a broker has access to a client, that means he has value. It is very difficult to get the ear of an owner, and where you have it, you have added value.
paragraphs.attribution: Hein Velema, May 2026

paragraphs: The critique above is not aimed at that work. It is aimed at incentives that travel undisclosed alongside the commission, and at the role ambiguity that asks one firm to answer to both sides of the same transaction. The standard this book applies is written disclosure. A party paid on completion, or by commission, can be engaged, provided the payment, its amount or rate, and who makes it are set out to the buyer in writing in advance, and the party’s role in the transaction is named. The buyer can then weigh the advice against the payment. The independence test in chapter 9 is built on the same rule.
Chris Cecil-Wright, founder of Cecil Wright, on the panel at the Superyacht Investor London forum in April 2026, located the broker’s value precisely:

paragraphs.text: We operate in the ‘information and confidence delivery’ part of the ecosystem. All the deals we’re doing offline are the ones where the value is. AI doesn’t know the nuance of the deal.
paragraphs.attribution: Chris Cecil-Wright, founder, Cecil Wright (Superyacht Investor London, April 2026)

paragraphs.text: The captain’s role in the structure

paragraphs: The captain is one of the most important hires an owner makes. Many owners make it early; chapter 9 sets out why the independent adviser, the lawyer and the surveyor should come first. The captain is involved in yacht selection, survey, sea trial, crew recruitment, management company choice, supplier relationships, and the day-to-day operating budget. They also bring a career and a network: prior owners, yards, brokers, relationships that pre-date the current employment. The role concentrates a great deal of authority and trust in a single individual, and the owner is well served by mapping the captain’s wider professional background before the appointment rather than discovering it later.

paragraphs.text: If you accept a fee for giving out the work, how can you still audit the quality of the result you are directly responsible for? You can’t. So for me it’s not really a question.
paragraphs.attribution: Capt. Pavlos Filippakis, Master Mariner (Class 1 Unlimited, Ice Class), May 2026

paragraphs: Andrew Roch, founder of Yacht Crew Recruitment and Training and a co-designer of the Yacht Owner Representative Programme with SYBAss, applies the same argument to the management-company tier. Writing in Superyacht News in June 2026, Roch documents the post-1990s shift in which large-yacht management companies migrated from administrative support into operational and financial control, drawing decision-making authority away from the captain on board and into shore-based offices. Responsibility for the vessel remained with the master; the authority that should accompany it did not.

paragraphs.text: The authority the role implies and the authority the role carries have come apart almost completely, and the captain is left holding a position that has been quietly emptied of its substance.
paragraphs.attribution: Andrew Roch, Founder and CEO, Yacht Crew Recruitment and Training (Superyacht News, June 2026)

paragraphs: On Roch’s reading the cost of that hollowing-out shows up first in psychological safety on board, and the most capable crew, those with employment options elsewhere, are the first to leave.

In interview, the candidate who pushes back, asks hard questions about intended use, and is sceptical of the timeline is the one to keep talking to; chapter 7 covers the hire in full. Capt. Filippakis, interviewed for this chapter, suggests one question that opens the subject of a captain’s network without making it adversarial: which brokers and yards the candidate knows best, and how those relationships began.

paragraphs.text: What independence means

paragraphs: Several firms describe themselves as independent. The word does meaningful work in some cases and is decorative in others. The full six-element independence test is set out in chapter 9 and applied to the publisher on the colophon. The questions are: contingent earnings, and whether they are disclosed in writing; equity or referral relationships; published counterparty list; transparent fees; appropriate professional indemnity; named, accountable principals.

The independent adviser is the person the buyer engages first, pays directly, and relies on to act for the buyer across an acquisition, a new build or a refit. This book uses “independent adviser” and “owner’s representative” for the same role. The adviser carries the project at principal level: scope, budget, programme, the contract, and the relationships with brokers, yards and suppliers. The role is not that of a broker, a project manager, a yacht manager or a captain; each of those is part of the team the adviser helps the buyer build. Chapter 5 describes the work on a new build, and chapter 9 sets out how to test and hire the adviser.

paragraphs.text: Before the first broker

paragraphs: Engage an independent adviser before any broker. Engage independent legal counsel, not the broker’s preferred firm. Engage an independent surveyor, not the seller’s. Pay all three directly. It is the cheapest insurance available. A party who objects to this arrangement has told you something useful about themselves.

04-acquisition-process.title: The acquisition process
04-acquisition-process.standfirst: From shortlist to closing in 12 to 24 weeks, with five decision points where most of the costly errors are made.
paragraphs: Once the decision to buy is made and the adviser team is in place, a brokerage acquisition takes 12 to 24 weeks and turns on five decisions: the shortlist, the scope of the pre-purchase survey, the sea trial, the VAT and flag position, and the terms of the contract at closing.

paragraphs.text: The shortlist

paragraphs: Most first-time buyers see 12 to 30 yachts before shortlisting three to five. The visit phase is where brokers add genuine value: they have walked the inventory and know what is rough and what is tight. It is also where they learn the buyer’s budget, intended use, timeline and family involvement, which shape every later recommendation.

Two habits protect the shortlist. First, keep the budget figure with the independent adviser. Brokers on both sides of a sale are usually paid from the seller’s commission, which rises with the price (chapter 3). Written disclosure tells the buyer how a broker is paid, but a budget figure shared with the broker can still become the floor of the negotiation. Give the broker the use case, size band and propulsion preference, and let them fit yachts to it. Second, walk yachts with the independent adviser alongside the broker; the adviser is looking for things the broker is not paid to find.

The shortlist should be three to five yachts, ideally from at least two brokerages. A shortlist drawn entirely from a single broker’s central-agency book is narrow by definition. The independent adviser can run a parallel scan against the entire market.
Boat shows are part of the visit phase, not the closing phase, and brokers say so on the record. Will Christie at the Palm Beach show in March 2026:

paragraphs.text: In almost 25 years in the industry I’ve only ever sold two boats directly off a boat show. The life of a broker is one of almost constant disappointment.
paragraphs.attribution: Will Christie, Palm Beach International Boat Show, March 2026 (Superyacht Investor)

paragraphs: The closing happens offline, in the weeks after the visit, with the buyer’s advisers in place. A buyer who signs an MOA in the closing hour of a boat show has signed on the seller’s timetable rather than their own.

paragraphs.text: Pre-purchase survey

paragraphs: The pre-purchase survey is the buyer’s main piece of technical due diligence, and the one most easily compromised by a buyer in a rush, in love with the yacht, or relying on the seller’s most recent class survey.

A proper survey on a 40m yacht runs 4 to 7 days afloat plus haul-out, costs USD 25,000 to 60,000, and involves an independently-engaged surveyor (not the broker’s), a class society inspector where applicable, and a paint, electrical, and mechanical specialist as scope demands. Recognised surveyors include Ward & McKenzie and Patton Marine. A surveyor the broker suggests may be entirely sound. Ask in writing whether they have worked for the broker or the seller, and instruct and pay them directly.

What the survey catches: corrosion, structural issues, paint condition, mechanical wear, electrical compliance, generator and HVAC condition, hull damage history. What it commonly misses: forthcoming class survey costs, latent design defects masked by patch repairs, hidden system modifications, and the full maintenance history.

The surveyor produces a report with deficiencies categorised by severity. The buyer has three options: walk away, renegotiate, or proceed. The usual response is to renegotiate, because any deficiency the survey finds and the price does not reflect is one the buyer pays for after closing.

paragraphs.text: Sea trial

paragraphs: The sea trial happens after the survey, typically on the same yard visit. Standard MOA terms allow 4 to 8 hours at the seller’s expense. The buyer brings their own captain candidate, surveyor, and a chief engineer where propulsion is central to the use case.

paragraphs.text: The surveyor tests whether the boat matches the specification. The captain tests whether she handles the way she’ll need to handle at three in the morning, in weather, with a tired crew.
paragraphs.attribution: Capt. Pavlos Filippakis, Master Mariner (Class 1 Unlimited, Ice Class), May 2026

paragraphs: What is being tested: handling, stability, vibration, noise at various engine loads, anchoring and ground tackle, navigation and comms, autopilot and control systems, comfort underway, and any failure mode the survey did not catch. Common failures: vibration at certain RPM bands, poor noise insulation in master cabin underway, unmaintained navigation electronics, stabilisers that work at one heel angle and not another.
If the trial reveals issues, the renegotiation continues. If not, the next step is closing.

paragraphs.text: VAT, flag, and registration

paragraphs: The VAT regime and the flag shape the cost of ownership for the next decade, and both can end up being settled in a hurry at closing.

They are also not separate from each other. The VAT regime, the flag, and the ownership structure the yacht sits inside are one decision with three parts, and settling them together before contracts are exchanged is far cheaper than unpicking them afterwards, when the exposure can be a liability calculated on the value of the yacht. Simon Roberts of Quadrant Group sets out that sequencing, and how early it has to happen, in chapter 9, where the yacht lawyer and structuring adviser are the second hire, before any contract is reviewed.

Value-added tax (VAT) regime. The default is full VAT on purchase: 20 percent in France, 21 percent in Spain, 22 percent in Italy. On a EUR 4 million yacht the bill is EUR 800,000 to EUR 880,000. Three legitimate routes can reduce or remove VAT on the yacht itself, and a fourth applies to refit works.

The French Commercial Exemption (FCE) eliminates VAT entirely if its conditions are met (commercial registration, full-time crew, length above 15 metres, at least 70 percent of voyages in the previous calendar year leaving French territorial waters, and charters at the quay fewer than half of all charter contracts). Maltese leasing no longer uses a length-based table: under guidelines of 12 March 2020, VAT on the lease follows documented use inside and outside EU waters, and the European Commission closed its infringement case that October. Italy moved to a comparable effective-use test from 1 November 2020, and leasing remains available where use can be evidenced. The fourth route, Spanish inward processing, concerns refit rather than purchase. A non-EU yacht refitted at a customs-site shipyard, with authorisation in place before the works begin, is exempt from the 21 percent VAT on the works, provided the procedure is followed through to the yacht’s departure from the EU. Time under inward processing does not count against the 18-month temporary admission period. Chapter 6 sets out how it works and where compliance rests.

Each option carries a compliance burden, and the choice should rest on the buyer’s own legal advice rather than on the broker’s preference. Hill Dickinson, Watson Farley & Williams, Ince, Stephenson Harwood and Reed Smith all publish comparative analysis. The buyer engages counsel directly, usually on the independent adviser’s introduction, with any relationship between the firm and the broker or seller disclosed in writing.

Flag state. Major options are the Cayman Islands, the Marshall Islands, Malta, and the other Red Ensign Group registers (UK, Isle of Man, Bermuda, Gibraltar, BVI, Jersey, Guernsey, and others), of which Cayman is itself one. The choice depends on owner residence, intended cruising area, charter intent, financing requirements, and the family office’s broader structuring preferences. Cayman and Marshall Islands dominate the over-30m segment. From 29 October 2026 a Malta-flagged yacht in private use can also be granted a US cruising licence, as Cayman and Marshall Islands yachts already could. The licence is issued by a US port director for up to twelve months, removes formal entry and clearance at each US port, and does not permit charter or change the yacht’s VAT position.

The technical baseline is the yacht code. The UK MCA Code of Practice for the Safety of Large Commercial Sailing and Motor Vessels (LY1, 1997) was rebranded as the Red Ensign Group (REG) Yacht Code in 2017 after successive revisions. Malta published its first national yacht code in 2006; the Marshall Islands followed in 2013. All three have been updated within the last two years to incorporate SOLAS Alternative Design and Arrangements (ADAs), the route by which innovative designs and alternative fuels (methanol, hydrogen, hybrid configurations) reach certification. Phil Noad of Cayman Registry argues that a harmonised IMO yacht code would not serve the segment; the dynamic competition between national yacht codes is what allows new technology to reach delivery ahead of IMO timelines. The recently formed Yacht Safety and Environmental Consortium (YSEC), under the International Association of Classification Societies (IACS), is the likely vehicle for cross-flag standardisation of base rules without erasing competitive variation (Phil Noad, in The Superyacht Report, Q2 2026).

One threshold shapes yacht design more than any other: 500 gross tonnage. At 500 GT a commercially operated yacht takes on the full SOLAS construction and fire package, the full ISM Code with shore-based management, the ISPS security regime, and a heavier manning scale. Of the 1,093 yachts in the 2026 Global Order Book, 932 measure under 500 GT, and designers build to the line: Gregory C. Marshall reports that 20,000 of the 64,000 design and engineering hours his studio billed in a year went on “squeezing yachts to measure under 500gt”. Inside that envelope, MLC accommodation minimums and Tier III exhaust after-treatment keep taking volume; Thom Conboy of Ocean Independence, a broker, puts the combined cost at 25 to 50 GT, or 5 to 10 percent of the yacht. Jack MacNally of Foreland Marine, the publisher of this reference, argues in The Superyacht Report (issue 230, September 2026) that the requirements anchored at 500 GT do real safety work, and that the defensible complaint is narrower: gross tonnage measures enclosed volume, while the risks the rules police scale with people and operation. A buyer with charter intent should read any design near 499 GT, and any later refit, against that line.

The flag does not settle every jurisdictional risk. The 58.5-metre Royal Huisman motor yacht Phi, which flew the Maltese flag, has been detained in London under a direction made by the UK Secretary of State for Transport on the evening of 28 March 2022 and delivered to her master the next morning, shortly after the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Her beneficial owner has not been designated under UK sanctions; the detention rests on his connection with Russia, and it has outlived the Transport Secretary who issued it, several governments and several legal challenges. The UK Supreme Court dismissed the owning company’s appeal on 29 July 2025, and the owner’s team has said it intends to take the case to the European Court of Human Rights. The point for a buyer is narrow: a state can detain a yacht in its waters whose owner is not personally sanctioned, whatever flag she flies, and a challenge through the courts can take years (Capt. Guy Booth, in The Superyacht Report, Q2 2026).

On a 40 metre yacht, tax compliance, structuring and the upkeep of the owning company run about EUR 35,000 to 110,000 a year, and flag administration and class society fees about EUR 15,000 to 40,000 more, EUR 50,000 to 150,000 in all. Flag and class fees also sit inside the operating compliance cost in chapter 7, which adds ISM, MLC and the management company’s compliance work, so they should be counted once. These costs recur every year and are not part of the purchase price.

paragraphs.text: The EC Guidance Note for Pleasure Craft of 30 April 2026 and Italian ADM Circular 11/2026 remain the working guidance into 2027: no minimum time outside the EU between Temporary Admission periods, and in Italy proof of reaching international waters ends a period. From 10 July 2027 the EU Anti-Money Laundering Regulation requires traders in high-value watercraft to carry out customer due diligence on the buyer and its beneficial owners, and to report every sale of a watercraft for non-commercial use at EUR 7.5 million or more to the national financial intelligence unit (chapter 3). Two 2026 developments that bear on the holding structure, the EU court’s ruling on trusts in the Sailing Yacht A case and Switzerland’s register of beneficial owners, are noted in chapter 9.
Closing

paragraphs: Closing itself is procedurally straightforward. MYBA MOA signed at heads-of-terms with deposit (typically 10 percent), closing 30 to 60 days later with balance, transfer of title, delivery, and a brief acceptance period (24 to 72 hours) during which the buyer can reject for material non-compliance with specification.

The errors are upstream, not at closing. By closing, the buyer has either negotiated the right contract or has not. The right contract has clean title warranties, an inventory matching what was sold, agreed deficiencies remediated or priced, an acceptance protocol that gives time to verify, and a governing-law clause that is not the seller’s home jurisdiction.

paragraphs.text: The five most common pitfalls

paragraphs: Five common pitfalls:

1. The broker-introduced surveyor. The broker suggests a surveyor whose work they know. The recommendation may be sound, but the surveyor’s independence has not been tested. Engage your own surveyor through your independent adviser.

2. The closing rush. Another buyer is interested, the marina slot is being lost, prices are about to move. An early close suits the seller and the parties paid on completion; the buyer carries whatever was not checked. Three further weeks of due diligence cost little against what they can find.

3. Inadequate survey scope. The buyer accepts a quote that excludes paint, electronics, or full mechanical inspection because the seller’s recent class survey “covered it.” Class surveys are not buyer-side surveys.

4. VAT regime defaulted to broker recommendation. A structure the broker recommends may be the one the broker’s usual lawyer handles, and it may not suit your use pattern. The VAT decision is worth a separate written opinion from counsel the buyer engages directly.

5. Closing without a competent technical handover. The seller’s captain knows the yacht; the buyer’s captain (often newly hired) does not. A 3 to 5 day handover with both captains and the chief engineer present surfaces issues that a paper specification does not.
A buyer who avoids these five will not have bought a perfect yacht, but will have bought one whose flaws they understand.

05-new-build-versus-brokerage.title: New build versus brokerage
05-new-build-versus-brokerage.standfirst: The choice between building and buying turns on three things: how much risk the buyer carries, when the capital is committed, and the quality of the buyer’s representation.

paragraphs.text: The two paths

paragraphs: Brokerage is the purchase of an existing yacht. Time from offer to delivery is typically 6 to 12 weeks; capital is concentrated at closing; the yacht is a known quantity to the extent the survey reveals it. The buyer takes the seller’s specification, build quality, wear and tear, and accumulated maintenance debt. The risk is assessed once, at survey, and accepted.

New build is commissioning a yacht to specification from a shipyard. Time from contract to delivery is 24 to 36 months for semi-custom and 36 to 60 for fully custom. Capital is committed in stage payments: typically 20 to 30 percent at signature, further instalments against build milestones, and a balance at delivery. Most of the price is paid before the yacht is delivered (see the first contract point below). The yacht is bespoke; everything from hull form to door handles is specified by the owner and the design team.

The cost premium of new build over a comparable brokerage hull is typically 30 to 50 percent at entry, narrowing to 15 to 25 percent at delivery as the brokerage hull depreciates and the new build hits the market. Over a five-year hold the gap closes further, and yachts from builders such as Feadship, Lürssen, Royal Huisman and Vitters hold their value better than most of the market.

paragraphs.text: Where new build risk concentrates

paragraphs: The published case record concentrates new build risk in three patterns: governance on the buyer side, yard financial condition during the build, and yard pricing too low to be credible. All three are addressable with the right representation team and contract structure.

Project Somnio, the 222 metre residential vessel associated with Carl Le Souef and Captain Erik Bredhe, generated a UK High Court ruling in January 2025 (Winch Design Limited v Le Souef [2025] EWHC 120 (Comm)) that Le Souef was personally liable for GBP 733,750 in unpaid invoices, the court finding that the special purpose vehicle (SPV) he had argued was the contracting party would not have been read as such by any objective bystander. The lesson for first-time buyers: contracting personally, or with SPV structuring that does not survive litigation, leaves the principal directly exposed. The fix is set at heads-of-terms by counsel, not after the dispute.

A second governance case on the published record comes from Jack Inglis at ULTIMAR. Writing in Superyacht Investor in October 2025: a semi-custom new build where the owner deputised a family-office CFO with no maritime expertise as owner’s representative. The delivery snag list exceeded 1,200 items against the family office’s reported figure of around 100, and the yacht was sold after a single season. Inglis’s summary of the pattern: “quantity does not mean quality, speed just equals more problems.”

paragraphs.text: A snag list is not a list of broken things, that is the mistake people make. You can have 300 cosmetic snags and sleep perfectly well, or you can have 15 critical commissioning issues and lose the first season. The real issue is never the number, it is understanding the difference between quantity and consequence.
paragraphs.attribution: Jack Inglis, May 2026

paragraphs: Inglis’s warning to first-time buyers in a period of larger and more complex builds is that vessels poorly overseen during construction return to the yards for warranty works faster than they were delivered.

paragraphs.text: The real measure is not whether a yacht has a two year warranty; it is how much of that period is spent enjoying the yacht versus fixing it.
paragraphs.attribution: Jack Inglis, May 2026

paragraphs: The yard-side pattern, less covered in trade press, has recurred through the 2020s: a yard runs into financial difficulty mid-build, and the owner is presented with a choice that is not really a choice. Inject additional capital, sometimes as equity in the restructured business, or face the yacht stalling, the supplier chain freezing, and the work-in-progress becoming an asset of the insolvency. Jack MacNally of Foreland Marine, the publisher of this reference, counted some 25 yard insolvencies across the custom and semi-custom fleet since 2000 in a review for The Superyacht Report (issue 230, September 2026), arriving in three clusters: 2009 to 2012, 2015 to 2018, and 2020 to 2026. Outcomes for buyers turned on structure more than on merit. Oyster’s 26 in-build customers were made whole in 2018 only because a buyer took on the whole company; at Christensen in 2015, suppliers’ liens on the named hulls ranked ahead of the buyers; Perini Navi’s largest in-build exposure, EUR 54 to 56 million, went into the 2021 bankruptcy as an ordinary unsecured claim. Buyers holding enforceable guarantees or registered title generally kept their boat or their money; buyers holding neither queued with the other creditors. In the TISG proceedings of 2026, set out below, a court suspended the guarantees as well, at least provisionally.

Nobiskrug, the German builder of Sailing Yacht A, is the clearest example. Then under Tennor Group (Lars Windhorst), the yard filed for insolvency in December 2024 alongside FSG. Lürssen acquired the assets in early 2025; the yard was integrated into the neighbouring Lürssen-Kröger facility, over 95 percent of the combined workforce transferred under a transfer-company mechanism, and suspended in-build projects (including a 62 metre yacht) moved to Lürssen for completion. Owners with hulls in the yard at insolvency faced direct exposure: contracts novated to the acquiring entity, terms renegotiated, in some cases additional payments requested to cover trustee costs.

Italian Sea Group’s 2026 restructuring (Admiral, Tecnomar, Perini Navi, Picchiotti, NCA refit) extended the logic into procedural protection. On 20 April 2026 the Court of Florence confirmed protective measures retroactive to the 16 March filing for a maximum four months. The order prevented shipowners from terminating in-build contracts during the restructuring window: from the buyer’s perspective a court-mandated commitment to a counterparty whose financial condition had changed since signature. The court partly revoked the measures on 10 June 2026. On 1 July the group filed for a court-supervised procedure with reported debts of around EUR 400 million. On 6 July the court confirmed new protective measures and, provisionally pending a hearing on 22 July, barred owners from terminating even for the yard’s own breaches or calling their refund guarantees, and barred the issuing banks from paying out on guarantees already called (TISG disclosure, 7 July 2026, as reported by MacNally). In August the group opened a sale process to investors, with binding offers due on 15 October 2026.

The buyer pays stage payments forward; when the yard’s financial condition deteriorates, those stage payments become creditor positions in someone else’s insolvency. Refund guarantees protect a portion of the exposure in principle; in practice, particularly under non-tier-one bank wrappers, they are less reliable than the contract suggests. Norton Rose Fulbright’s commentary on Chinese-bank refund guarantees expiring within one month of cancellation is widely cited; the timing of insolvency proceedings rarely lines up with the guarantee window. Benjamin Maltby, a partner at Keystone Law, sets out what separates a reliable guarantee: a bank of high credit standing, preferably independent of the yard and its group; payment on written demand without investigating the dispute; all instalments covered, with interest; validity running to delivery plus a margin. Even then it repays only the sums paid, not lost use, financing costs, or owner-supplied items, and it responds only to a valid termination and a correctly presented demand. The instrument is also rarer and more fragile than buyers assume. “The majority of shipyards simply don’t have the credit lines available to them to be able to arrange refund guarantees,” in the words of Alex Sayegh of HFW, so the yards strong enough to provide one tend to be the ones least likely to get into financial difficulty. Where a guarantee exists, its expiry is commonly set against the contractual delivery date, so cover can lapse as a late build reaches its riskiest period, and a material variation agreed without the guarantor’s consent can void it (MacNally). The Florence order of 6 July showed that a restructuring court can freeze even an on-demand guarantee.

Three workstreams the buyer’s team handles in advance. Yard financial due diligence at heads of terms: recent published accounts, parent structure, order-book composition, and litigation history form part of standard pre-contract assessment. Refund guarantee credit quality carries the same weight as any other contract term. And the buyer decides in advance, with counsel, what to do if mid-build distress produces an equity-injection or accelerated-payment proposal, so the decision is made before the pressure arrives. The contract can record that decision: a right to information on the yard’s financial condition at set intervals, a right to suspend payments on named warning signs (missed supplier payments, a rating downgrade, a covenant breach, a shareholder change), and step-in rights over the unfinished hull, materials, and design files so the vessel can be completed elsewhere (Maltby). The difficulty is timing. Termination clauses respond to formal events, the opening of proceedings or the appointment of an administrator, and yards file late. “Even where the owner can see that the yard is in trouble, it cannot take action under the contract,” Linda Roxburgh of Wikborg Rein wrote in 2024. The signs come earlier: prices cut to win deposits, senior technical staff leaving, suppliers asking whether the last instalment has been paid. TISG published its financial position monthly under a CONSOB order throughout its decline, and MacNally knows of no credit-monitoring service that reads such filings on a yacht buyer’s behalf.

The third pattern is distinct from yard financial distress: a price below what the build can credibly be done for. Hein Velema, the first president of SYBAss, puts this test first when assessing a yard (see his interview in this chapter). A yacht’s build cost is direct cost plus overhead, and the overhead is not money the yard wastes on itself; it is what produces a quality boat. Margins on top-tier construction are thin to begin with, and a buyer who has done diligence on one yard will know roughly what they are. When another yard quotes fifteen percent below for a comparable build at similar margins, the arithmetic does not work, even if, as Velema notes, brokers sometimes describe such a quote as a great deal.

The historical case is documented in the public association history of the Superyacht Builders Association (SYBAss). New yards arrived in the market with very deep capital in the early 2000s, sold large hulls at prices the founding yards (Feadship, Lürssen, Benetti) could see were below cost, and discovered as much on delivery. In at least one cited case, seven hulls had already been sold by the time the first was completed. The SYBAss eligibility rule of three delivered hulls over forty metres came directly out of that period. Once a yard has delivered, it knows what the boats actually cost.

paragraphs.alt: The 60 metre Baltic 111 sailing yacht Raven photographed in profile under sail
paragraphs.caption: Raven, Baltic 111. A new build delivered against a contract whose change-order procedure, refund guarantee, and dispute forum had been settled at heads of terms.

paragraphs.text: The contract is where it happens

paragraphs: A new build contract governs USD 30 to 200 million of capital across two to five years. It settles every variation, dispute and question of interpretation in the period during which the yard holds the cards.

Kevin Laverty of Hill Robinson, in a BOAT International feature sponsored by his firm (September 2025), describes the relative thinness of yacht-construction contracts as drafted. Coming from oil and gas, where a project of comparable cost is documented in several ring binders, he found a 33-page contract governing the build of a 77 metre yacht.

paragraphs.text: Page count means very little on its own. What matters is whether the contract actually controls risk.
paragraphs.attribution: Jack Inglis, founder, ULTIMAR, May 2026

paragraphs: Standard shipbuilding forms exist (SAJ, AWES, NEWBUILDCON, SHIP 2000); the SAJ form, published by the Shipbuilders’ Association of Japan, is most used globally and “thought to favour the shipyard” in unamended form. But the European yards that matter (Lürssen, Feadship, Oceanco, Royal Huisman, Heesen, Sanlorenzo, Benetti) do not contract on any of those. They contract on heavily customised in-house templates drafted by their counsel, with English law and London arbitration grafted on. Maltby gives the reasons: English law is predictable, arbitration awards can be easier to enforce than court judgments, and arbitration is private where court proceedings are public. The first draft places most of the risk on the buyer, and buyers do better by selecting a few essential changes than by redrafting everything.
A buyer who signs without specialist shipbuilding counsel is negotiating a bespoke document drafted entirely by the yard’s lawyers, with no standard form to measure it against.
Ten specific points an inexperienced representative gives away at signature:

1. Stage payment loading. Commercial shipbuilding lawyers put the share of the price paid before delivery at 40 percent or more (Watson Farley & Williams). In custom yacht work it is routinely well over half, and on some projects as much as 90 percent (MacNally, citing Port Royal Group). Aggressive front-loading suggests the yard is short of cash to start the build. On yard-standard contracts the milestone that releases each instalment is often self-certified: the yard states the stage is complete and invoices, and nothing requires an independent surveyor to have looked. On a EUR 12 million build paid in five stages over 30 months, the owner’s exposure just before launch is around EUR 9 million, three quarters of the price, held against a contract and a record of payments (MacNally).

2. Refund guarantee credit quality. Tier-one bank pay-on-demand guarantees are materially better than surety wrappers. Chinese-bank refund guarantees commonly expire one month or less after cancellation, forcing immediate arbitration (Norton Rose Fulbright).

3. Liquidated damages cap. Industry typical: 1 percent of contract value per week of delay, capped at 5 to 10 percent of contract sum. After the cap, the yard owes nothing further (Hill Dickinson, citing Triple Point Technology v PTT [2021] UKSC 29).

4. Force majeure burden. English law requires the yard to prove “but for” causation under Classic Maritime v Limbungan [2019] EWCA Civ 1102. Yard drafts are often looser, and an inexperienced representative may accept them.

5. Change order procedure. Without a defined procedure with pre-agreed unit rates and third-party quote rights, “the owner is open to being forced to pay for change orders or emergent work at a unit rate much higher than in the original contract” (Stephenson Harwood, Sean Gibbons).
6. Defect notification deadlines. Typically 14 days from discovery, with failure to notify potentially extinguishing the claim entirely (HFW).
7. Warranty length. Standard 12 months. Negotiable to 24. The buyer has to ask.

8. Cancellation thresholds. SAJ standard: 150 days post-delivery date or 180 days total delay (Jiangsu Guoxin v Precious Shipping [2020] EWHC 1030). Bespoke yacht contracts replicate but with negotiable thresholds.

9. Title position during construction. Some yards (Feadship cited) retain title until delivery; others transfer progressively. This determines who carries insolvency risk and who has repossession rights. Where the yard keeps title and becomes insolvent, the buyer is an unsecured creditor and the refund guarantee is the main recourse. Progressive title is stronger on paper than in practice; the contract should require the hull and materials to be marked and kept separately, inspection rights, insurance with the buyer named, a right of entry and removal on default, and a local-law opinion on whether the transfer will be recognised (Maltby). Title is decided by the law of the build country, whatever law the contract chooses. In Italy the yard owns the yacht during construction unless the parties agree otherwise in writing, and that agreement protects the buyer in an insolvency only once it is transcribed in the registro navi in costruzione at the local Harbour Master’s office; Germany keeps a shipbuilding register for the same purpose (MacNally, citing Jay Tooker of HFW and PG Legal).

10. Dispute forum. English law plus London Maritime Arbitrators Association (LMAA) arbitration is the practitioner default. Inexperienced representatives sometimes accept non-English law or non-LMAA seats that materially weaken the buyer’s position.

Specialist review of the yard’s draft at heads of terms costs a small fraction of the sums these clauses govern. In the case in this chapter, a change-order clause without unit rates let the yard take about EUR 5.2 million in variation margin on a EUR 95 million contract, more than the fee range given below for an independent representative across a whole build.

paragraphs.text: What an owner’s representative does

paragraphs: Chapter 3 defines the owner’s representative, whom this book also calls the independent adviser: paid by and accountable to the owner, and carrying the project at principal level. On a new build that means scope, contract, budget, programme, and the relationship with the yard above the day-to-day. Project managers, brokers, yacht managers and captains are part of the team the representative builds.
The work runs across four phases.

Pre-contract. The representative scopes the acquisition or build with the owner, sets the budget envelope, identifies the candidate yards or hulls, and runs the comparison against the owner’s actual use case. The strongest cost saving in any project is made here, before the contract is signed.

Contract. The representative leads for the buyer in heads-of-terms drafting, working alongside specialist shipbuilding counsel. Stage payments, refund guarantee credit quality, change-order procedure with pre-agreed unit rates, warranty length, dispute forum, and title position during construction are the points where inexperienced representation is most exposed.

Build, refit, or post-acquisition. The representative supervises against the contract: weekly reporting, milestone payments tied to defined deliverables, snag-list control, and the technical workstreams that determine quality at delivery. On a major project the representative appoints a project manager for the day-to-day; on a smaller one, carries both roles.

Acceptance and warranty. The representative runs the snag list to closure, manages sea trials against the contractually named noise and vibration limits, prosecutes warranty claims, and produces a delivery record that holds up in any subsequent insurance, sale, or refit conversation.

Representatives typically come to the role from a senior operational career, often as a yacht captain or chief engineer, where they have already managed budgets, contracts, crew, refits and the technical workstreams from the operating side of the yacht.
