paragraphs.text: Why the yards founded YORP

paragraphs: SYBAss announced the Yacht Owner Representative Programme (YORP) in June 2023 and ran the first course at Benetti in Livorno that July: four courses totalling more than 200 hours, of which Unit 40 is the only mandatory course for the most experienced practitioners. The Yacht Owner’s Representative Register (YORR) followed at The Superyacht Forum in Amsterdam in November 2024, administered by the Malta-based Superyacht Alliance for Professional Standards, with a CV audit “to eliminate inflated CVs” and a code of conduct. The transitional route for experienced representatives closes on 30 June 2027; after that, a register listing means either the full programme or verified projects plus Unit 40.

The four courses run from the shipyard outwards: how the yard builds and is financed, the representative’s own tasks, the legal layer, and the leadership that carries a difficult project to delivery. The register adds a check on what applicants claim: a detailed application form, a reference that is called, and projects reclassified where the two disagree. Velema, now Secretary General of the Alliance, describes the curriculum and the vetting in his own words in the interview in this chapter.

SYBAss member yards (Lürssen, Feadship, Oceanco, Heesen, Royal Huisman, Vitters, Baltic, Abeking & Rasmussen, Codecasa, CRN, Benetti, Sanlorenzo) collectively build roughly two thirds of yachts over 40 metres. According to Velema, the programme began because those yards reported that some owner’s representatives had no clear idea of what the role was or what the yard expected of them.

The yard side has begun hosting the programme directly. Lürssen welcomed the Superyacht Leadership Academy to its Hamburg shipyard in April 2026 to deliver Unit 40, framing the visit on its own corporate channel as evidence that owner’s representatives “play an equally critical role” alongside the shipyard.

paragraphs.text: The whole purpose of the Alliance is to promote professionalism. The Owner’s Representative is not the only role in the industry that needs to be made clearer. We are very happy to support work outside the Alliance that is contributing to the education and clarity of the people in the industry.
paragraphs.attribution: Hein Velema, Secretary General, Superyacht Alliance for Professional Standards, May 2026

paragraphs.text: The owner’s representative market

paragraphs: Chapter 3 sets out how the people around a yacht transaction are paid, and the written-disclosure standard this book applies. A new build adds one payer to that picture: the yard, which may pay commission to the firm advising the buyer. Firms working as owner’s representatives paid only by the owner, with no broker commission and no yard affiliation, are a small group. They include A2B Marine Projects, ULTIMAR, Divergent Yachting, Mariner Technical Services, Occam, and Foreland Marine, the publisher of this reference.

paragraphs.text: Disclosure. The publisher, Foreland Marine, is an independent yacht consultancy led by Jack MacNally and Daniel Marks, with a team of 20+ industry consultants. Foreland is SYBAss accredited and YORR registered. The independence test in chapter 09 applies just as it does to any other firm a reader is considering.

paragraphs: The code of conduct that runs alongside the register is about behaviour rather than knowledge. An example commonly cited is the ten-percent commission on the tender. It is not an absolute prohibition: a representative who takes that commission can still register, provided the arrangement and the amount have been disclosed to the owner in writing in advance. That meets the written-disclosure standard set out in chapter 3. The Alliance’s general position, in Velema’s words, “is that you do not”.

Brokerage houses with new build arms include Edmiston, Burgess, Y.CO, Ocean Independence, Camper & Nicholsons, Fraser, Cecil Wright, and Moran. Burgess Technical Services describes its work as “independent, objective oversight”; Burgess is also one of the largest brokerages. Cecil Wright, a brokerage, topped the Spear’s 2025 Yacht Advisers ranking and is acting as owner’s representative on the 83m Feadship Project Solent, due for delivery in summer 2027.

Where a brokerage’s technical department acts for the buyer on a build, the same group may have introduced the yard and may be paid commission by it. That is the new-build form of the dual role. The buyer should ask, in writing, whether any part of the group will be paid by the yard or its suppliers on the project, how much, and on what.

Yacht management companies extending into new build include Hill Robinson, Döhle Yachts Technical Services, and Wright Maritime Group. Naval architects acting as owner’s representatives include Vitruvius (Briand), Reymond Langton, Espen Oeino, Bannenberg & Rowell, Andrew Winch, and Malcolm McKeon (MMYD). A design firm in that role may also have a continuing commercial relationship with the yard, and the same written disclosure applies.
Family-office-focused entrants are post-2023: Ikonic Yachts, Superyacht Partners, Praxis Group, Oak Group, Morpho Luxury Asset Management.

Fees at the major firms (Edmiston, Burgess, Cecil Wright, Y.CO, Moran, Hill Robinson) are not published, and independents rarely publish percentages either. The anecdotal practitioner range for independent firms is 1 to 3 percent of build cost, or fixed fees of EUR 1 to 3 million over a 36-month build on a EUR 100 million project. Brokers acting as owner’s representatives are typically paid through yard commission of around 5 percent, about EUR 5 million on the same project. Owners, in Velema’s words, “do not always know how much, or on what”. Under the standard in chapter 3, the buyer should have the figure and its source in writing before engaging the firm.

paragraphs.text: The wider build team

paragraphs: An owner’s representative on a serious new build leads a team. The specialist disciplines around the lead role determine how much of the yard’s first-draft position the owner is able to test.

Maritime counsel from a specialist shipbuilding firm leads the legal workstream. Hill Dickinson, Watson Farley & Williams, Clyde & Co, Stephenson Harwood, HFW, Reed Smith, Norton Rose Fulbright, and Ince are the regularly named firms. They cover the construction contract, change-order procedure, warranty terms, title during construction, finance and security, and flag and ownership structure.

Mechanical and propulsion advisors review engine selection, gearbox, shaft line, propeller geometry, and any hybrid or diesel-electric integration. On larger hulls the propulsion package is a multi-million-euro line item the yard’s first quote may not have optimised for the owner’s intended use.

Vibration and acoustic engineers run finite-element models early in the build, then sea trial measurements at acceptance, against published comfort-class targets (Lloyd’s Register PCN, RINA Comfort, ABS Habitability) and noise envelopes (sleeping-space and saloon typically 45 to 55 dB(A) under cruising load). Missing the comfort-class targets at delivery is one of the most expensive defects in the warranty period; the usual cause is that the analysis was not run early enough to influence shaft line, mounts, and structural detailing. The two scopes are normally bid as a paired engagement.

Paint surveyors are their own discipline. Yacht paint is a six- or seven-figure line item on a 50 to 80m hull. Wrede Consulting, IMS Paint Surveying, and a small number of independents write the specification before the yard quotes, then run progress inspections and cure tests. Paint is a frequent subject of post-delivery warranty disputes, and independent paint oversight is a cheap way to avoid them.

Interior consultants, engaged independently where the lead designer has yard affiliation, validate joinery, fabric and leather grades, climate behaviour through commissioning, and the long lead-time items that drive the back end of the schedule. Class society consulting validates the path to certification at Lloyd’s Register, DNV, ABS, or RINA, including any yard-proposed innovations that may interact with the regulatory pathway.

The total cost of the assembled team on a EUR 100 million build runs EUR 2 to 4 million across a 36-month project, against a build cost the yard’s first-draft contract typically allows to drift by 5 to 15 percent.

paragraphs.text: The decision

paragraphs: For a buyer considering new build, the threshold tests are these.
First, do you have a 7 to 10 year hold horizon? If not, brokerage; the new build cost premium does not amortise over a shorter hold.

Second, is your intended use pattern genuinely specific to the yacht (size, layout, propulsion, range, operational profile)? If a brokerage hull within a reasonable search window can deliver 80 percent of your use case, brokerage. Custom is for the residual 20 percent that genuinely matters.

Third, can you commit to building the team that new build requires? Independent owner’s representative engaged before contract, specialist shipbuilding counsel from a top firm, technical due diligence on the yard’s current order book and financial condition, and a willingness to push back against the yard’s first-draft contract on every point that matters. If commitment to all four is not in place, brokerage tends to be the calmer path.

If all three answers are yes, new build at a SYBAss member yard gives the buyer a yacht specified for its use, from a builder whose work holds its value. Without those conditions, it tends to be one of the more expensive ways to acquire a yacht. The case in this chapter is for the conditions, not against the path.

06-refit.title: Refit
06-refit.standfirst: Where ownership cost concentrates, where the yacht’s condition is renewed, and where the relationship between owner and yard is most often tested. The chapter also covers the alternative to a refit: selling the yacht.
paragraphs: A yacht’s life is divided into refit cycles. Every five years a class survey forces structural and systems work; every ten years the cosmetic and major-systems condition demands substantive overhaul. Refit is where ownership cost concentrates, where the yacht’s condition is renewed, and where the relationship between owner, yard and project manager is most often tested.

The global refit market was USD 2.9 billion in 2025 supporting roughly 6,000 active vessels (Future Market Insights), and while capacity has expanded modestly the fleet has grown substantially. The result is tightening lead times at the dominant yards.

paragraphs.text: When to refit, when to sell

paragraphs: The decision to refit assumes the owner intends to continue owning. For a 12 to 15 year old yacht facing major refit, the alternative is sale and reacquisition. The arithmetic depends on three variables: strategic fit with the owner’s continued use case, the cost of a comparable replacement, and how the post-refit yacht will depreciate against the alternative.

A practitioner rule of thumb, not a market rule: if projected refit cost exceeds 30 percent of pre-refit market value, and the yacht is not strategically irreplaceable for the use case, sale is usually the better decision. Below 30 percent, refit normally is, although the threshold is rough and the calculation is bespoke.

The owner who refits the wrong side of that threshold takes on a project whose total cost runs well above the post-refit yacht’s market value. The owner who sells a strategically-fit yacht on the basis that “the refit was looking expensive” will spend more on the replacement and lose crew continuity that takes years to rebuild.

A third option, less considered, is the transformational refit: a rebuild that extends, reconfigures, or repositions a hull as a step-change in capacity rather than a maintenance cycle. A well-chosen 55 to 65 metre brokerage hull rebuilt at scale can deliver the volume and amenity of a 70 to 75 metre new build at a 30 to 50 percent capital saving against comparable new construction, delivered in 12 to 18 months rather than three to four years. For an owner weighing a EUR 70 to 100 million new build several years from delivery, the transformational refit on a known hull is a third path worth examining before the new-build contract is signed. The conversation typically begins with the captain, who knows both the asset and the owner well enough to know when to raise it (Justin Olesinski, in The Superyacht Report, Q2 2026).

paragraphs.text: Selling the yacht

paragraphs: Selling is the other answer to the refit question, and it needs the same preparation. The Refit Advisory Group asks owners to decide early how long they will keep the yacht, because selling in two years, keeping her for ten, or passing her on each calls for a different level of investment. A yacht approaching her five-year class survey is sold with that work ahead of her. Chapter 4 notes that a pre-purchase survey commonly misses forthcoming class survey costs, so a well-advised buyer asks about them directly. A seller with the class status and expected scope in writing answers with documents rather than leaving the buyer to estimate.

Records are part of what is sold. In the group’s words, “Good records also have resale value. A yacht with a complete history surveys better, sells faster and needs less expensive exploratory work at her next refit.” The papers this chapter recommends for a refit serve a sale as well: the condition record, the Deferred Items Register, class and flag papers, as-built drawings and manuals, and the final account of the last yard period. Chapter 4 lists the full maintenance history among what a pre-purchase survey commonly misses; a seller who supplies it closes that gap.

Most sellers appoint a broker under a central agency agreement, a fixed-term and exclusive mandate under which one broker markets the yacht and other brokers introduce buyers through it. MYBA publishes a standard form. Clyde & Co’s Guide to Superyacht Law (fourth edition) names three terms to look for: the minimum marketing activity the broker commits to, the commission payable after the agreement ends, and the governing law, noting that agreements governed by Florida law can be tough on a seller. The seller’s own lawyer should settle how long commission after termination runs and which buyers it covers.

The seller pays the commission from the proceeds. Chapter 3 sets out the two norms in use: on a EUR 28 million sale, about EUR 1.7 million under the MYBA sliding scale and EUR 2.8 million under the US flat 10 percent. Where another broker introduces the buyer, that broker is paid from the seller’s commission, typically half of it or a little less. Sellers do not always know which norm applies, so the scale and any split belong in the listing agreement. If the central agent also finds the buyer, it acts for both sides. The book’s standard for that, as for any commission, is written disclosure of the payment and the role (chapter 3).

Price governs time on market. Northrop & Johnson’s figures for the third quarter of 2026 show that yachts of 24m and above that sold had been listed for an average of 445 days. Asking prices were cut 1,949 times in the first nine months of the year, and the heaviest average cuts, 31.1 percent, fell on yachts aged 25 to 29 years. Chapter 2 explains what these figures measure. A buyer’s adviser reads a listing’s time on market and its price cuts against them, and the seller should price with the same figures in hand.

The sale contract is usually the MYBA Memorandum of Agreement, described from the buyer’s side in chapter 4, and it binds the seller in the same terms. The buyer pays a deposit, typically 10 percent, on signing. The seller’s warranties are narrow. Andrew Charlier of HFW describes them as the right to sell and delivery free of mortgages, liens and other claims, with exclusion clauses ruling out any warranty on condition beyond what the agreement states. Liens are discharged before closing (BOAT International, September 2025). Under the 2021 MYBA E-MoA the seller also warrants that no undischarged tax or VAT liability has been incurred (Penningtons Manches Cooper, April 2022), so the evidence of the yacht’s VAT status should be ready before listing. The warranties are usually backed by a guarantee, in a form MYBA provides, from the beneficial owner or a company on its behalf; Ezio Dal Maso of Stephenson Harwood notes that its scope, cap and expiry are settled deal by deal (September 2026).

Where the yacht is owned through a company, the buyer can buy the yacht or the company. Charlier notes that buying the company means taking on all its liabilities, and that most buyers decide it is cleaner to buy the yacht as an asset through their own structure. A seller who plans to sell the company should expect that preference, and take tax advice on both routes before heads of terms are agreed.

The seller’s team follows the same rule as the buyer’s. The seller’s own lawyer reviews the listing agreement and the MOA, and an independent adviser paid only by the seller can assemble the records, the class position and the pricing evidence before the yacht is listed.

paragraphs.text: Refit cost benchmarks

paragraphs: A five-year survey or major refit typically runs 5 to 15 percent of insured hull value, depending on scope. The working ranges per metre below come from the archive of more than 30 refit projects managed by Foreland Marine, the publisher of this reference. Annual maintenance is a yearly cost; the two refit figures are the cost of the project.

Annual maintenance: EUR 2,000 to 8,000 per metre a year. Mid-life refit: EUR 10,000 to 30,000 per metre for the project. Major structural refit: EUR 40,000 to 100,000 or more per metre for the project.

On a 50m yacht a major structural refit therefore costs EUR 2 million to EUR 5 million for the project (50 × EUR 40,000 to 100,000). Full-scope projects involving extension, re-engining, or substantial cosmetic and systems renewal sit at the top of that band and above it, typically USD 5 million to 10 million.

The Refit Advisory Group, an independent, not-for-profit group of owner’s representatives, captains, technical and project managers, surveyors, and yard professionals, of which Foreland Marine, the publisher of this reference, is a member, sets the refit inside the yacht’s whole cost cycle in its Owner’s Refit & Lifecycle Guide (version 1.0, November 2026, to be published in Q1 2027). In its members’ experience a major refit period within a five-year cycle can cost as much as a year’s operating budget. The guide keeps four budgets apart, annual maintenance, planned refit, regulatory works, and owner upgrades, so the owner can see whether the yacht is being looked after or simply spent on. Equipment fitted at the same time tends to fall due at the same time, and a ten-year cost profile drawn at purchase shows the clusters an annual average hides; giving every critical system a known end-of-support date turns obsolescence into a scheduled line item rather than a failure. Costs outside the yard invoice (accommodation, travel, storage, security, temporary services) belong in the budget before the yard period starts.

paragraphs.text: Refit reserve is an annual line, not a lump sum. The running cost calculator carries it against your own size, type, region, and use intensity.

paragraphs: Mediterranean berth fees during refit run EUR 400 to 800 per day for a 40 metre hull. Northern Europe berth fees run EUR 600 to 1,200. Mediterranean skilled labour runs EUR 45 to 75 per hour with specialists at EUR 80 to 120. Northern Europe runs 20 to 40 percent more across both labour categories.
These figures come from project archives, not published rate cards; MB92 and Pendennis do not publish day rates.

paragraphs.text: The 30 to 50 percent overrun pattern

paragraphs: Industry consensus is that refit projects routinely run 30 to 50 percent over the original quote. Dockwalk documented an extreme case, a sixfold overrun on a 1967 Camper & Nicholsons refit (USD 1 million budget, USD 6 million actual).

The overrun has two sources. Part of it is work that could not be seen when the quote was made: a yard quote based on visual inspection cannot anticipate everything found when the deck is opened, the engine room stripped, or the bilges scrubbed. That part is real cost, and no contract removes it. The rest comes from loose specification and weak project management, which let unpriced work and changes of mind through without control. Maltby describes the overrun the same way, as partly a pricing problem and partly a contract problem. The first part is budgeted for; the second is contained.

Practitioners size the contingency reserve for the first part: 10 to 15 percent for known scope, 15 to 20 for opened-up vessels, 20 to 25 for older hulls opened for the first time. A reserve on that scale covers a well-managed refit, which typically lands within 10 to 20 percent of the quote, but not the full 30 to 50 percent pattern. On a EUR 3.2 million quote, a 20 percent reserve is EUR 640,000, while a 40 percent overrun is EUR 1.28 million, leaving EUR 640,000 unfunded.

Benjamin Maltby, a partner at Keystone Law, puts the containment in the contract. It should assume hidden defects will appear and set rules for them at the outset: a pre-works survey that records the yard’s findings as a baseline, fixed-price work separated from provisional sums and day-rate work, and no additional work or charge without a written variation order signed by a named person for the owner. Each variation states its cause, price, and effect on programme and on the other trades, and the owner keeps the right to decline it, take a second opinion, or have the work done later or elsewhere.

The contract type should follow how well the scope is defined. The group’s Owner’s Toolkit sets out three: fixed price, which works when the scope is fully defined and leaves the yard carrying overruns within it; cost plus, which suits an uncertain scope and leaves the overrun with the owner; and target cost with shared savings, which needs a mature scope and gives both sides an incentive to save. Most owners are offered only the first two. Where target cost fits, the group finds it changes yard behaviour more than any amount of supervision.

In the publisher’s project archive, a well-managed refit at a competent yard with experienced owner-side representation typically lands within 10 to 20 percent of the original quote, and a poorly managed one at the extremes. Representation is one factor among several, with the yard, the contract and the state of the hull.

The overrun is also measured in time. A late yard period costs far more than the extra yard days: lost use, repositioning, crew retained without a programme, guest plans unwound and, on a charter yacht, revenue forgone rarely appear on the invoice and usually outweigh it. The Refit Advisory Group’s answer is a realistic timeframe agreed on a defined scope, delay penalties asked for, and anything that moves the date treated as a variation.

paragraphs.text: Two yard models

paragraphs: Two yard models shape everything that follows. Full-service yards take the project as a single contract, manage the trades in-house, and deliver at an agreed milestone. Service yards (also called marina yards) provide the facility, haul-out, and infrastructure, while the owner contracts the trades directly through the project manager. The same metre of dock is billed very differently between the two.

STP Palma (Servicios Técnicos Portuarios), Port of Palma de Mallorca, is the best-known service-yard example. Owners and their project managers contract paint, mechanical, electrical, and joinery directly with resident specialists; STP provides the haul-out, hardstand, and perimeter services. The model rewards experienced project management and suits owners wanting full visibility of every contract line. Lauderdale Marine Center and parts of Marina Port Vell Barcelona operate on similar lines.

Full-service yards (MB92, Pendennis, Lusben, Astilleros de Mallorca, Amico & Co, Rybovich) carry the integration risk and price for it. Service yards (STP, LMC, Marina Port Vell, sections of Astilleros de Mallorca) shift integration responsibility to the owner-side team and are typically less expensive at the line-item level for owners with capable project management. Neither model is inherently better; the right one depends on the buyer’s representation, the project scope, and the buyer’s tolerance for direct contract management.

The service-yard model carries a liability gap the line-item saving does not show. Each trade is liable only for its own contract and its own work, so when one trade’s work interacts with another’s and something goes wrong, each can point at the other and the burden of proving which caused the loss falls on the owner. In Maltby’s words, “nobody holds overall responsibility for coordination unless the owner has appointed someone and given them that duty in writing.” The owner’s trade contracts should be drafted as a set, under the same governing law and dispute forum.

paragraphs.text: Refit yard capacity

paragraphs: The over-30m refit market is concentrated in four geographies: Western Mediterranean (Spain, France, Italy), Northern Europe (UK, Netherlands, Germany), Eastern Mediterranean (Turkey), and the US Eastern Seaboard. Most large-yacht refits land at a few dozen yards in those regions. The data spread for this chapter lists them by region, with location, yard model, capacity and ownership. Ownership has moved recently: Squircle Capital took full ownership of MB92 in March 2026, Amico & Co joined the Amico Marine group in May 2026, and Rybovich belongs to Safe Harbor Marinas, part of Blackstone Infrastructure since April 2025.

BOAT International’s February 2026 expert roundtable (Manuel Di Tillio at Amico & Co, Gianni Paladino at Lusben, Txema Rubio at MB92) discussed Mediterranean capacity in detail; it is paywalled. Its published introduction cites BOATPro data showing the global fleet up 38.7 percent within the past decade, and describes refit capacity as tightening. Top European yards are typically booked 12 to 24 months ahead for major refits; US East Coast lead times are shorter but tightening, particularly at Rybovich and Derecktor.

A first-time owner planning a major refit in 2028 or 2029 should therefore book as far ahead as the chosen yard’s order book runs: up to 24 months at the top European yards, less at US yards and for smaller scope. The cheapest yard is rarely the best choice. The better one has a track record on similar yachts and a project manager who has handled comparable scope.

paragraphs.text: Spanish IPR and the VAT economics of refit

paragraphs: For non-EU flagged yachts, Spanish Inward Processing Relief (IPR), the régimen de perfeccionamiento activo, is the principal VAT procedure for refit in EU waters. It is a separate customs procedure from temporary admission, which covers the yacht’s use in EU waters and ordinary repair and maintenance but not a structural refit.

The mechanism: a non-EU yacht enters Spanish waters under temporary admission, which runs for up to 18 months. For the refit it is placed under inward processing at a customs-site shipyard, and time under inward processing does not count against the temporary admission period. Spanish VAT law exempts the works, and the parts and services that go into them, from the 21 percent VAT, for private and commercial owners alike, provided the procedure is followed through to the yacht’s departure from the EU.

On a EUR 5 million refit the saving is approximately EUR 1.05 million. The compliance burden is real (customs-site shipyard, bonded works, documentation, re-export evidence) but the saving more than justifies it. MB92, Astilleros de Mallorca, and several smaller Spanish yards are equipped for IPR. The relief is not automatic: authorisation must be in place before the works begin, sought through the yard or an agent with the correct customs status. The owner is often told that the yard handles the VAT, but compliance rests with the owner, in whose name the procedure runs. If it is not followed, the customs authority can treat the yacht as released for free circulation, with VAT due on the works and potentially on the yacht itself, plus interest and penalties (Maltby).

The French Commercial Exemption also removes VAT on refit work where its conditions are met. Those conditions, and Maltese and Italian leasing, are set out in chapter 4. The choice should rest on advice from a yacht lawyer with VAT expertise who is not the yard’s preferred counsel.

paragraphs.text: Insurance during the works

paragraphs: The hull insurance market, including its response to the loss of Bayesian in 2024 and current rates, is covered in chapter 7. During a refit the relevant insurance is builder’s risk, not the cruising hull policy. Builder’s risk is taken out by the yard with the owner’s interest noted, covering loss or damage during the works up to redelivery. A noted interest gives the owner much less than named-insured status: possibly no direct right to claim, no right to see the full policy, and no protection if the yard breaches a policy condition (Maltby). Before the haul-out the owner obtains the full wording rather than a certificate and confirms co-insured status with a waiver of subrogation, a sum insured that reflects the whole vessel rather than the works, the exclusions (faulty workmanship, defective design, pre-existing damage, delay), the deductibles and who bears them, and cover in the water, on the hard, during lifts and tests, and in transit between subcontractor sites. The owner’s own hull and machinery policy usually suspends or limits cover in the yard, so the broker confirms in writing what remains in force.

paragraphs.text: What “superyacht standard” should actually mean

paragraphs: “Superyacht standard” is the phrase the trade routinely deploys to describe finishes, tolerances, and workmanship that are, in practice, vaguely defined and easily disputed. The contract that says the work will be carried out “to superyacht standard” is a contract that has not been written. A usable specification cites the manufacturer’s data sheet, the relevant ISO standard, or both. Nine items it should name:

Paint dry film thickness (DFT). Awlgrip and Alexseal manufacturer TDS define the DFT range per coat (typical Awlgrip topcoat 75 to 125 microns per coat, total system 200 to 450 microns). The contract cites the TDS version and requires gauge measurements at agreed intervals.

Paint application conditions. TDS specify ambient temperature (typically 18 to 29°C for Awlgrip topcoat), relative humidity below 80 percent, and surface temperature at least 3°C above the dew point. Controlled-atmosphere spray cells are the only consistent route; the contract should require atmospheric logging.
Drying and recoat windows. Manufacturer-specified recoat windows in hours at given temperature and humidity. The contract references the TDS version and requires sign-off at each recoat point.

Vibration. ISO 6954:2000 and ISO 20283-5 are the marine standards; engine and gearbox manufacturers (MTU, Caterpillar, MAN, Rolls-Royce, ZF) also specify drivetrain tolerances. The contract cites both.

Noise levels. ISO 6954 and the International Maritime Organization (IMO) MSC.337(91) apply to crew areas; owner cabins are held tighter. Practitioner standard for master cabin underway: 45 to 50 dB(A) at design cruising speed. Sea trial noise mapping required.
Whole-body vibration. ISO 2631 sets comfort limits. Practitioner targets at master cabin underway and at anchor are typically below 0.315 m/s² RMS.
HVAC. ISO 7547 gives the design conditions; manufacturer TDS (Heinen & Hopman, Westmar, Drews Marine) specify duct velocity (typically below 2.5 to 3.0 m/s in occupied spaces) and air change rates.
Hydraulic and stabilisation. Quantum, Naiad, ABT-TRAC, Veem TDS set the operational envelope and noise limits in dB(A) at the equipment. Isolation mounts specified in writing.

Surface preparation. Holiday testing on metallic substrates, profile measurement on prepared steel (typically Sa 2.5 cleanliness, 50 to 75 micron profile), humidity-controlled preparation. Skipping it is a common cause of premature paint breakdown between years three and seven.

A well-drafted contract names each in writing with TDS versions and ISO editions cited. The phrase “superyacht standard” does not appear, because it cannot be enforced. No regulator, class society, or trade body defines it, and Maltby’s view is that a court would treat it as too vague to enforce or fall back on an implied term of reasonable skill and care, a low bar that turns on expert opinion. A specification that cites Awlgrip TDS revision X or ISO 6954:2000 gives buyer, surveyor, and arbitrator something to measure against; it reduces dispute, accelerates sign-off, supports warranty claims, and produces a delivery record that holds up in any subsequent insurance, sale, or refit conversation.

paragraphs.text: How to get a refit right

paragraphs: Three habits separate well-managed refits from the rest.

First, scope. Define the work in writing before the contract is signed, with specific deliverables, materials, and finishes, and the named manufacturer and ISO references above. The vague clause is the source of the overrun. Project managers who insist on detailed scope at the start are more expensive to engage and considerably cheaper across the project.

The scope includes the tonnage. Remeasurement is triggered by a substantial variation in gross tonnage, which class guidance reads as anything over 1 percent; on a 499 GT yacht that is five gross tons, roughly one enclosed deck module. The Red Ensign Group’s 2024 tonnage guidelines confirm that permanent deck additions cannot be excluded, and caution that exclusions accepted by one flag may not be accepted by another. For a commercially operated yacht, a refit that crosses 500 GT brings the commercial package the hull was engineered to avoid. A naval architect’s tonnage calculation, included in the scope before it is signed, takes about a day (Jack MacNally of Foreland Marine, the publisher of this reference, in The Superyacht Report (issue 230, September 2026)).

The Refit Advisory Group adds four habits to the scope work. A design freeze date, set in advance and known to everyone, after which every change is priced, programmed, and approved as a variation; its members name scope creep as the owner’s biggest single pain point. Work sorted into what is mandatory (class, flag, safety, and law), what is recommended and why, and what is the owner’s call, each with its reasoning and the consequence of not doing it. A Deferred Items Register recording what was not done, why, and when it will be reviewed, because almost every serious dispute comes down to a conversation nobody wrote down. And long-lead items (engines, switchboards, glass, teak, joinery, rigging, anything needing class approval) decided early, often before yard selection, because the critical path usually runs through procurement rather than labour. Critical areas are opened first, not halfway through the yard period.

Second, milestone payments. Tie payments to defined deliverables (paint cells completed to specification, engine reinstall completed and vibration measured, sea trials passed against the named noise and vibration limits) rather than to calendar dates.

Third, weekly site presence. The owner-side team on site at least one day per week through the works. Weekly reporting, with photographs and snag lists, surfaces issues at the point they can still be addressed cheaply, rather than at delivery when they cannot. The Refit Advisory Group recommends a recorded handover between captain and refit manager in the first fortnight, to capture what the captain knows and nobody has written down; otherwise the yard rediscovers it at yard rates. The crew plan needs the same attention: immigration status and Schengen limits checked early, leave and a return date agreed, and the captain and engineers not left running the yacht and the refit at once.

One further term belongs in the contract before work starts: what happens if the project falls into dispute while the yacht is still in the yard. Under English law a repairer usually holds a possessory lien over a yacht it has worked on, and yard terms often extend it by contract to all sums owed, including disputed amounts and sums under other contracts. A lien is not title, but the leverage is considerable, particularly in charter season. Release is normally against security, with the disputed sum paid into escrow or a solicitor’s client account or covered by a bank guarantee. Maltby’s advice is to settle these terms at the outset, because the owner who first reads them under pressure has already lost most of the bargaining power.

The end of the project belongs in the contract too, because redelivery is not completion. The Refit Advisory Group lists what to settle at the start rather than at the end, when everyone wants to go home: snag close-out to an agreed process, sea trial against written acceptance criteria, retention and its release, the warranty period and process, as-built drawings and manuals, spares, crew familiarisation on new systems, class and flag paperwork, and a final account with every variation accounted for. Two simpler measures settle many disputes before they start: a condition record of time-stamped photographs and video before yard entry, and written confirmation that the owner’s hull cover, the yard’s liability, and the yard’s hot-work conditions meet without a gap.

A note on titles. On a small refit one person carries both the owner’s representative role (the independent adviser defined in chapter 3) and the project manager role. On a major refit the two separate: the representative is the strategic role at the contract, budget, and yard-relationship level, paid by and accountable to the owner; the project manager is the tactical role, on site daily, running the interface with the yard, the trades, and the surveyors, and producing the weekly reporting. Under the service-yard model, where the owner contracts trades directly, the two roles separate earlier and the project manager typically reports to the representative. Either arrangement works, provided both roles are paid by the owner and any other payment either receives is disclosed to the owner in writing (chapter 3).

A representative on a EUR 5 million refit typically charges EUR 200,000 to EUR 400,000, or 4 to 8 percent of project value. In this chapter’s case, an adviser engaged late in the project for EUR 95,000 recovered about EUR 410,000 under the yard’s warranty.

07-operations.title: Operations
07-operations.standfirst: The captain hire does more than any other decision to settle whether the yacht is a pleasure or a source of friction. The other four decisions of year one compound across the hold.
paragraphs: The operation of a yacht runs from delivery to sale. Over a typical seven-year hold, cumulative operating spend approaches the purchase price, and the team is often introduced through the broker who sold the yacht. Five decisions taken in the first year shape how the yacht runs and what it costs: the captain hire, the management company, the insurance arrangement, whether to charter, and the refit reserve. Crew structure follows largely from the captain and the size of the yacht, and regulatory compliance is usually delegated to the management company. Each decision compounds across the hold.

paragraphs.text: The captain hire

paragraphs: The captain is the most consequential hire an owner makes. A good captain runs a quiet, professional yacht with low crew turnover, predictable maintenance costs, and few unpleasant surprises. A poor one produces the reverse, and the cost shows in turnover, maintenance and surprises.

The pay differential between a good captain and a competent average one is small; the operational differential is large. YPI Crew’s 2026 salary guide places captain pay on a 50 to 60 metre yacht at EUR 10,000 to 16,000 per month. Quay Crew records average pay from EUR 6,000 on a 20 to 24m yacht to over EUR 25,000 on a 100 to 119m vessel; the 70 to 79m bracket saw a 7 percent increase on its 2023 survey, and 63 percent of the captains surveyed are on time-for-time rotation.

Erica Lay of EL Crew Co reports that captains in the 50 to 70 metre range with proven leadership, commercial awareness and crew-management capability now command salary uplifts of EUR 1,500 to 4,000 per month above traditional benchmarks, with rotation, bonuses and improved leave structures on top. The combination of technical capability and what Lay calls emotional intelligence is rare, and it is where the pressure on cost sits.

The test this chapter proposes is to hire the candidate who pushes back hardest. The captain who asks about actual use pattern, family, tolerance for transit days and refit reserve budget is showing how he or she will work; easy agreement in the first interview rounds is pleasant in the room but tells the owner less. Erica Lay adds a step: check references “not just from other owners and managers. Dig deeper, and talk to the crew who’ve worked under their leadership.”

paragraphs.text: A Captain has to reduce the operating risk profile of his vessel and fighting for that is part of the job.
paragraphs.attribution: Capt. Pavlos Filippakis, Master Mariner (Class 1 Unlimited, Ice Class), May 2026

paragraphs: The independence question applies here as well. A captain recommended by the broker who sold the yacht may keep a relationship with that broker, which benefits if the captain later passes on charter requests or acquisition referrals. Hiring through a recruitment agency engaged by the owner’s independent adviser removes that link, and any continuing relationship a candidate has with a broker, yard or management company can be disclosed in writing at interview, as the checklist for this chapter asks.

paragraphs.text: Do not just hire the best captain on paper. Hire the one who can manage you. A good captain runs the yacht. A great captain manages the entire ecosystem around it, including the owner.
paragraphs.attribution: Erica Lay, founder and director, EL Crew Co

paragraphs.text: Crew structure by size

paragraphs: A 40 to 50 metre motor yacht operates with 8 to 14 crew: captain, chief officer, bosun and one to two deckhands, chief engineer, second engineer above 50m, chief stew, two to six interior crew, chef. Variance sits mainly in the interior team; deck and engineering numbers move little within a given length.

Above 50 metres the structure expands to 12 to 20 crew, above 60m to 18 to 26, and above 80m to 25 to 35. Numbers scale roughly linearly to 70m and faster above. Sailing yachts run a third or so lighter at every length (chapter 8).

Crew is the largest single line in the operating budget, at 30 to 40 percent of total cost (chapter 1). Post-pandemic inflation produced double-digit annual increases at junior levels through 2021 to 2023; junior crew pay has since plateaued, while senior crew pay continues to rise.

Time-for-time rotation, which Quay Crew records for 63 percent of the captains it surveyed, is now expected on senior-crew programmes. In Erica Lay’s words, rotation “is no longer a perk”; in many cases “it is the price of entry to access the top end of the market”. On her reading, roles without rotation take longer to fill, attract a narrower and often less experienced pool, and are far more likely to need refilling within 12 to 18 months. Capt. Pavlos Filippakis, who supports rotation, names the cost the salary line does not show: two captains with different standards on documentation, crew discipline and what gets escalated. “Without active management, you get drift, and crew quietly optimise for whichever captain is onboard.” A management team that oversees standardisation, he says, is what makes it work.
Lay’s view is that the real cost of crew lies in turnover, retraining and disruption rather than in junior pay, so retention is where the owner can most affect it.

paragraphs.text: Captain and crew salary benchmarks for 2026, by position and yacht size, with the recruitment-side sources named.

paragraphs: Erica Lay names the most common cause of turnover as inconsistency from the top, whether it comes from the owner, the captain or the management structure. Crew, she says, can handle hard work, long hours and demanding programmes; what they struggle with is unpredictability and a lack of trust in leadership. Capt. Filippakis makes the same link from the captain’s side. Turnover follows the culture aboard, and the owner usually appoints the people who make or break it, mostly the captain, chef and chief stew.

paragraphs.text: A yacht is only the visible part. If you have a beautiful yacht but a bad ecosystem around it, it becomes an ugly yacht very quickly. Yacht ownership is not defined by the yacht; it is defined by the people, systems and infrastructure behind it.
paragraphs.attribution: Jack Inglis, founder, ULTIMAR, May 2026

paragraphs.text: The owner’s year

paragraphs: Most of this chapter concerns what the owner delegates, but the owner still has work to do. In the chapter 9 case, the adviser estimated that a 49m yacht would take 40 to 60 days a year of the owner’s direct attention, through season planning, refit scheduling, supplier conversations and crew matters, on top of 80 to 120 days of family use. Chapter 1 sets that time against the case for ownership.

Season planning is where owner and captain first test each other. In this chapter’s case, the captain the owner eventually hired had pushed back in interview on the proposed itinerary, because the transit times between the owner’s preferred destinations would compromise the maintenance schedule, and on a compressed autumn refit that would create cost later. He asked about the owner’s use pattern, the family’s actual behaviour on board and the budget envelope. Asked for the advice brokers and management companies rarely give, Erica Lay puts the same point from the recruitment side: “The best captains understand how to set boundaries, communicate clearly, and guide a first-time owner through decisions they have never had to make before.”

The budget is the other recurring conversation. In the chapter 1 case, the owner’s second yacht was bought with a team he paid directly at known rates, and its operating cost has run at 13 to 14 percent of original capex a year, inside the moderate-use band his adviser set out before he bought. On that yacht, the case records, he is unlikely to be surprised by an invoice. The refit reserve and the cost profile described at the end of this chapter belong in the same annual cycle.

The owner’s part is to hear advice that is inconvenient. In this chapter’s case, the captain has recommended against particular refit yards, suppliers and charter arrangements, and has recommended selling the yacht when the owner’s use had drifted from the use it was specified for. The owner did not sell, but took the advice as evidence that he had hired the right captain. Lay describes the cost of the opposite: “If you get that hire wrong, everything else becomes harder. Crew turnover increases, the onboard culture suffers, and the programme becomes reactive instead of enjoyable.”
