paragraphs.text: ISM, MLC, and flag state compliance

paragraphs: The International Safety Management (ISM) Code is mandatory for yachts of 500 gross tonnage and above that are engaged in trade, which in practice means charter. It requires a documented Safety Management System, a Document of Compliance held by the managing company, and regular audit. A privately used yacht is outside the mandatory regime whatever its size, although an owner can adopt ISM voluntarily, and some flags, Malta among them, offer voluntary certification. Yachts engaged in commercial operation also fall under the Maritime Labour Convention (MLC), which governs crew working conditions, contracts, hours, and welfare. Where they apply, both frameworks are binding and audited. Amendments to the Maritime Labour Convention in force since December 2024 require reasonable-cost internet access, free food and drinking water, and protective equipment in suitable sizes. Further amendments are expected to enter into force on 23 December 2027: they strengthen shore leave, define what repatriation must cover, and require measures against violence and harassment on board. For a charter yacht that means revised crew agreements and complaint procedures during 2027, normally handled by the management company.

Compliance is delegated to a yacht management company in most cases. Firms offering management include Hill Robinson, Burgess, Y.CO, Döhle Yachts, Moran, Edmiston, Camper & Nicholsons, Fraser, and Foreland Marine, the publisher of this reference. Several of them also broker yachts, so any referral between their brokerage and management sides falls under the written-disclosure standard in chapter 3. The management company maintains the SMS, files the regulatory paperwork, runs the audit cycle, and supports the captain on flag state interactions.

Flag state choice (covered in chapter 4) determines which regulator audits, which regulator’s manning rules apply, and which jurisdiction’s labour law governs crew contracts. Cayman, Marshall Islands, Malta, and the Red Ensign jurisdictions dominate the over-30m segment.

What compliance costs depends on how the yacht is used. For a 40 metre yacht in commercial operation, or one whose owner has adopted ISM voluntarily, the safety management system and its audits, MLC compliance, flag administration, class society fees and the management company’s compliance services typically run to EUR 80,000 to 200,000 a year on practitioner working ranges. Flag administration and class fees, about EUR 15,000 to 40,000 of that, are the same fees chapter 4 counts in its EUR 50,000 to 150,000 for tax, structuring and flag administration, and belong in a budget once. A 40 metre yacht in private use is usually outside both ISM and MLC, so its compliance cost is mainly flag and class fees plus whatever compliance work the management company is contracted to do. Chapter 1’s 2 to 3 percent of operating cost for regulatory and class compliance excludes the management fee, which it counts separately. Whichever applies, the operating budget should show compliance as its own line.

paragraphs.text: The insurance market, brokers and underwriting

paragraphs: After the captain, insurance is the operating decision with most money at stake. The hull policy alone covers an asset typically worth EUR 10 million to EUR 200 million, and the broker and the underwriting behind it determine, at claim time, whether the owner is made whole.

The market first hardened after sustained Lloyd’s yacht underwriting losses through the mid-2010s: in 2019 Sean Blue, AIG’s global head of watercraft, spoke of increases of 50 to 70 percent in the London market (BOAT International, November 2019). Rates rose again from 2022. The Lloyd’s yacht line ran loss ratios above 100 percent for several consecutive years (2015: roughly GBP 150 million premium against GBP 210 million claims), and only around 5 percent of yacht premium written returned a profit between 2011 and 2017. Rate increases had largely stopped by the first half of 2024, which Ollie Davis of PIB Marine, interviewed for this chapter, regards as the peak of the cycle. The market has since softened, though the rate reductions brokers published for 2025, Gallagher Specialty’s among them, describe commercial shipping hull and machinery rather than yachts. The typical hull rate for a well-maintained 40 to 50 metre yacht is 0.7 to 1.5 percent of insured value a year; smaller yachts and those in hurricane-exposed regions pay 2 to 5 percent.

Davis attributes the hardening chiefly to the pandemic and the war in Ukraine: spare-parts shortages, repair-cost inflation, yard capacity squeezed by sanctioned Russian hulls stuck in refit, and Covid-era cruising patterns that left more yachts than usual in the Caribbean and Florida through the hurricane season. Insurers built a premium stockpile against the risk that a repeat of the 2018 hurricane damage would land on a larger exposed fleet. He expects 2026 to be stable, with hull and machinery premiums flat or rising marginally with inflation, and P&I clubs continuing their usual 5 percent increases as more claims exceed USD 1 million. The softer market has one catch for owners. When the same yacht is presented to underwriters for several consecutive years, usually three or more times and by different brokers, Davis notes that underwriters can start declining to offer terms.

The Bayesian sinking in August 2024 (USD 150 million insured loss) prompted speculation of a fresh hardening cycle. Pantaenius’s Michelle van der Merwe, on the record: “I think everyone thought it was going to have more of an impact than it did.” Davis reports the same from the broker side: no significant rating increases across the large sailing yachts PIB Marine handles, the Bayesian hull being a design Perini has built several times but with a rig that is effectively a one-off. Where the market has responded, it has done so through surveys rather than rates.

paragraphs.text: What we have seen is an increase in underwriters’ and insurers’ requests for Risk Management Surveys. These are now being used to assess how crew procedures, training, and onboard management contribute to the safe day-to-day operation of the yacht. This represents a shift away from the more traditional focus on fire risk and watertight integrity alone.
paragraphs.attribution: Ollie Davis, PIB Marine, May 2026

paragraphs: The contingent risk is whether published findings from the Bayesian investigation ultimately attribute fault to the designer, builder, or naval architect. The precedent is Oyster’s keel-detachment losses, after which some insurers declined to quote on multiple Oyster models because they could not rule out recurrence. If Bayesian’s findings land on builder or designer responsibility, underwriter appetite for other vessels of the same provenance may be reassessed before any segment-wide rate signal moves.

paragraphs.text: The brokers, by relevance to the over-30m segment

paragraphs: Howden and Pantaenius are among the largest yacht insurance brokers in the over-30m segment, and AON Marine, Gallagher Specialty and Marsh also place substantial large-yacht business. PIB Marine (formerly Zorab Insurance Services), where Ollie Davis works, is a UK yacht specialist. For the owner, the practical step is at least three quotes from brokers with over-30m experience, each disclosing its commission in writing (chapter 9).

paragraphs.heading: The brokers, firm by firm
paragraphs: Howden Group has consolidated significant yacht-specialist capacity through acquisitions, building a London practice with strong access to Lloyd’s syndicates and European specialty markets. Operates across hull, P&I, war risk, builder’s risk, and charter cover. Strong on scale, underwriting access, and structuring for complex programmes; less personal than a specialist alternative for smaller, single-hull buyers.

Pantaenius (Hamburg, 1899) is the reference for European yacht insurance and one of the largest yacht-specialist brokers globally. Deep service capability, strong loss-management track record, yacht-only frame, disciplined coverage drafting. Relationships are weighted toward European underwriters; owners with heavy US East Coast use can sometimes access tighter US rates elsewhere.

AON Marine offers yacht insurance within a broader marine and corporate practice. Integrates with wider family-office programmes (aviation, other lines) where AON also holds the relationship; yacht-specialism depth varies by team.
Gallagher Specialty operates a strong yacht practice on the US East Coast (US fleet coverage, hurricane underwriting, US syndicate access). European depth is thinner than Pantaenius or Howden.

Marsh, largest broker globally by revenue, places yacht business through its specialty marine teams. Capital and reach for the largest hulls (above 100m) where bespoke structuring is required; yacht-specialist service depth varies.
PIB Marine (formerly Zorab Insurance Services) has long-standing partnerships with naval architects, designers, and project managers; depth closer to Pantaenius than to the global brokers.

Smaller yacht-specialist brokers and single-jurisdiction houses carry the rest of the segment. Selection here is mostly relationship-based; underwriting markets accessed are similar to the larger brokers.

paragraphs.text: The underwriting that sits behind the broker

paragraphs: The broker accesses the underwriters; the underwriting pays at claim time. Four points matter most.

First, the hull and machinery policy should be written on agreed value, not actual cash value. Under agreed value, the sum paid in a total loss is fixed in advance; under actual cash value, the insurer pays the depreciated market value, typically much less. The premium difference is small, but on a large hull the difference at claim time can run to tens of millions.

Second, the agreed value should reflect rebuild cost, not market value. A 50m yacht with a EUR 18 million market value may cost EUR 28 million to rebuild, and insuring at market value leaves the owner short after a constructive total loss. Brokers including Howden and Pantaenius offer agreed-value cover on a rebuild basis; ask for it and check the figure against a current yard quote.

Third, review the policy annually for coverage drift. Itinerary changes (US East Coast, charter introduction, new cruising area) trigger different coverage requirements. The broker who reviews proactively at renewal is meaningfully different from the broker who re-quotes the prior year.

Fourth, many deductible and warranty terms can be negotiated at quote stage, and the broker should push back rather than accept templates. Davis names four for first-time owners. Insurers increasingly add Actual Cash Value clauses on machinery, or higher engine deductibles, on yachts five years and older; well-documented maintenance logs, oil-sample results and manufacturer inspections at the prescribed intervals can often persuade underwriters to remove the separate machinery deductible, sometimes for a modest rise in the overall H&M deductible or the premium. A No Claims Discount offered upfront has to be repaid on non-renewal or after a claim, and is not normally worth taking. Mast, spars, sails and rigging (MSSR) deductibles and the inner deductibles on fixtures, emergency towing, tenders and personal effects can mostly be adjusted to the vessel’s actual risk. Standard tender-towing terms are often more restrictive than current practice supports, and monitoring systems from providers such as Yacht Trace have made extended towing more acceptable to underwriters.

paragraphs.heading: Who carries the capacity
paragraphs: Lloyd’s syndicates underwrite the majority of large-yacht hull capacity (active: CNA Hardy, Beazley, Brit, AIG, Liberty Specialty, Tokio Marine HCC, MS Amlin). AXA, Allianz, Generali, and Helvetia also underwrite directly on European-domiciled programmes.

paragraphs.text: The five lines of cover, on a typical large yacht

paragraphs: An over-30m programme typically carries five lines of insurance, each separately underwritten and renewed: hull and machinery, protection and indemnity (P&I), war risk, builder’s risk during refit or new build, and charter cover where the yacht is chartered. This chapter’s data spread sets out what each covers, what it typically costs and who writes it. War risk is often misunderstood. It covers unexpected damage from riots, uprisings, vandalism or political incident while the yacht is outside high-risk zones; entering a designated War Risk area needs an additional premium agreed with insurers in advance. Since the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, insurers have also issued seven-day notice of cancellation on hull and P&I cover for certain cruising areas, so the itinerary is checked with the broker before it is fixed.

paragraphs.text: Ironically, War Risks cover does not provide cover for you while you are in designated War Risk areas, which is something that is often misunderstood.
paragraphs.attribution: Ollie Davis, PIB Marine, May 2026

paragraphs: Builder’s risk, which covers the yacht in the yard during refit or new build, is usually taken out by the yard with the owner’s interest noted; chapter 6 explains why that gives the owner less than co-insured status and what to confirm before the works begin.
The difference in fee between a yacht-specialist broker and a generalist is small. The difference at claim time can run to eight figures, as the rebuild-cost example above shows.

Cover for sexual misconduct claims is a newer question. In a 2025 case, a crewmember who was sexually assaulted in English Harbour, Antigua, aboard a St Vincent-flagged yacht owned through a Marshall Islands LLC, had the vessel arrested at its Fort Lauderdale berth on a US maritime lien after the local authorities did not act. The case raises three points. Yacht liability policies routinely exclude sexual misconduct claims; where the exclusion is enforceable, the owner is personally liable for the claim and the defence. The maritime lien attaches at injury, travels with the vessel and is exposed the first time the vessel enters a US port; a foreign flag and an offshore SPV do not defeat an in rem arrest under 28 U.S.C. § 1333. US policies also contain strict notice provisions, and delay or concealment of an allegation can affect coverage. Supplemental sexual misconduct cover is available, some owners now buy it, and it is arranged with the broker before an incident, not after (Adria Notari and Ryan Melogy, plaintiff’s US maritime counsel, in The Superyacht Report, Q2 2026).

paragraphs.text: Charter operation

paragraphs: The decision to operate commercially through charter is separate from the decision to buy, and is best taken separately, even when the two are presented together.

Charter requires the right commercial registration, MLC compliance, a charter management company, and a charter brokerage relationship. The economics, as covered in chapter 1, are unfavourable for the median operation; most charter yachts subsidise rather than recover ownership cost.

Commercial registration is decided jurisdiction by jurisdiction; there is no single global licence. The regimes a first-time charter operator is most likely to meet, in France, Italy, Spain, Greece, Croatia, Turkey, Monaco, the Cayman Islands and Marshall Islands, Malta and the United States, are set out country by country in this chapter’s data spread. Two have changed recently. Spain has replaced its charter licence with an Affidavit of Responsibility filed with the Harbour Master, with 2026 as the transition year, and since February 2024 Greece has allowed some non-EU-flagged commercial yachts over 35m to charter under the e-Charter Permission. The VAT regimes that interact with charter, the French Commercial Exemption and Maltese and Italian leasing, are covered in chapter 4.

For a US owner, tax treatment is a further consideration. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed in 2025 and effective for assets acquired on or after 20 January 2025, permanently restores 100 percent first-year bonus depreciation for qualifying business yachts under Internal Revenue Code section 168(k). For a US owner whose yacht is documented and operated as a charter business, with charter use exceeding 50 percent and the hours and records that IRC section 469 demands, the depreciation deduction can be material against ordinary income in year one. The provision is generous on paper and audited tightly in practice. The arrangements are set with US tax counsel before contract, and the charter operation has to be real. The two-part Marine Money / BOAT International Monaco forum coverage in September 2025 contains the published numerics from US private bankers and yard counsel.

Whether charter pays is covered in chapter 1, using BOAT International’s case studies. Only one of the four showed a clear profit, a 60m concept modelled at 12 weeks rather than a trading yacht, and that depended on premium rates and on releasing the prime weeks.

For a first-time owner, charter is normally a poor decision in years one to three: the yacht has not established a charter reputation, and the crew are still settling. The default is private operation for three years, with a deliberate year-four decision based on actual usage and a projection checked against the chapter 1 cases.

paragraphs.text: Emerging cruising frontiers

paragraphs: Three frontier markets sit outside the conventional regime list. None was operationally ready for first-time owners in September 2026; each is worth tracking on a five-to-ten year planning horizon. The Knight Frank Wealth Report 2026 (“Wealth without borders”) and BOAT International are the references on all three.

Indonesia. 17,000 islands and extensive diving on the cruising-ground side. Strict local laws preventing foreign-flagged vessels from chartering, combined with thin marina infrastructure across the archipelago, currently deter commercial superyacht activity. Cruising privately is possible with the right agency support; commercial charter at scale is not. The watch item is regulatory, not technical.

Saudi Arabia. The Red Sea coast development from Jeddah to Aqaba, including the pro-yacht Amala project, is a state-backed land reclamation and resort programme targeting the segment. Some of the region’s strongest sailing weather and reefs sit on a coastline that did not previously accommodate foreign hulls. Build delays are widely reported; programmes are running ahead of facilities at this writing.

Japan. Active government investment in marine infrastructure, regulatory liberalisation for foreign-flagged visits, and port modernisation. The opportunity is real; the regulatory unwind is slow. A credible third Asia-Pacific destination alongside the established Southeast Asian routes on a five-year horizon.

A yacht intending to charter across multiple jurisdictions in a single season needs the right combination of flag, commercial registration, and country-by-country permits in advance. The charter management company normally coordinates; the owner should check that each intended cruising area is covered before season planning is finalised.

paragraphs.text: The five operational decisions of year one

paragraphs: In rough order of consequence:

1. Captain hire. Commit to interviewing five candidates minimum, all sourced through routes outside the broker’s relationship. The captain hired now will shape the crew, the maintenance and the budget for years.

2. Yacht management company. Choose it on its merits rather than by default from the broker’s recommendation, and ask in writing whether any referral fee passes between the management company and the broker (chapter 3). The management company is the long-running operational partner.

3. Insurance broker selection. Obtain quotes from at least three brokers with over-30m yacht experience; the main ones are named above. Ask each to disclose its commission in writing, and do not default to whichever broker the seller used.
4. Charter or private decision. Default to private for years one to three. The decision to charter is one to make deliberately, with the data of actual private use to inform it.

5. Refit reserve and capex planning. Build a refit reserve from year one. The five-year class survey and the ten-year refit come round on schedule, and an owner who has not built a reserve can find the cash short by year four. The Refit Advisory Group (chapter 6), of which Foreland Marine, the publisher of this reference, is a member, recommends in its Owner’s Refit & Lifecycle Guide (version 1.0, November 2026, to be published in Q1 2027) a ten-year cost profile drawn at purchase, with annual maintenance, planned refit, regulatory works, and owner upgrades kept as four separate budgets, so the years where major items fall due together are visible in advance.

08-motor-versus-sail.title: Motor versus sail
08-motor-versus-sail.standfirst: Sailing yachts and motor yachts of the same length differ in operating cost, crew, carbon and resale market, and hybrid drive now sits between them. The comparison is worth running before a first-time buyer defaults to motor.
paragraphs: The choice between sail and motor is often presented as a question of taste. For a buyer planning a decade of ownership, the two also differ in operating cost, carbon, the cruising they suit and the value they keep, and hybrid drive now offers a third option.

The market is asymmetric. BOAT International’s 2026 Global Order Book records 69 sailing yachts among the 1,093 on order, about 6 percent of units; Camper & Nicholsons and SuperYacht Times brokerage data places sailing yachts at around 18 percent of the active over-30m fleet. The leading sailing yacht builders (Royal Huisman, Vitters, Baltic, Nautor Swan, Wally) sit in a smaller category by units and a larger one by hold value.

paragraphs.text: Operating cost, line by line

paragraphs: A 50 metre sailing yacht runs meaningfully less than a 50 metre motor yacht of comparable build quality. The two are seldom costed side by side for a buyer. Practitioner ranges, from a Foreland archive of managed projects:

Fuel. A 50m motor yacht running 400 hours a year under way burns EUR 200,000 to 350,000 of diesel, about 110,000 to 270,000 litres at the EUR 1.30 to 1.80 a litre assumed in chapter 1. The archive range does not separate generator fuel at anchor and in port, which should be budgeted as its own line. A 50m sailing yacht operated mainly under sail burns EUR 60,000 to 120,000, about 33,000 to 92,000 litres.

Crew. On the archive figures, a 50m sailing yacht operates with 9 to 12 crew against 12 to 16 on a comparable motor in private use. Published guides suggest leaner minimums: YachtBuyer gives 8 to 12 for the 40 to 50m band, and 9 for a lean 50m crew. Variance on both sits mainly in the interior team. Sail-handling specialism on deck adds modest cost; the engine room runs lighter. Quay Crew 2025/26 records sailing yacht captain pay slightly below motor at equivalent length, although the experienced sailing yacht captain market is thinner.

Maintenance. Sailing yachts carry rigging and sail-wardrobe costs that motor yachts do not: full sail wardrobe replacement at 7 to 10 year intervals runs EUR 400,000 to 1.2 million, and standing rigging at 10 to 15 years runs EUR 250,000 to 700,000. Set against that, sailing yachts carry less main-engine wear, smaller stabiliser systems, and simpler hydraulic and HVAC loads, so net annual maintenance is broadly comparable; the cost shape differs. The Refit Advisory Group (chapter 6), of which Foreland Marine, the publisher of this reference, is a member, advises in the Owner’s Toolkit that accompanies its Owner’s Refit & Lifecycle Guide (version 1.0, November 2026, to be published in Q1 2027) that a sailing yacht be bought on its position in these cycles, not only on its condition: a well-presented yacht with rigging in its ninth year has a large known cost arriving shortly. Unstepping the mast is a project inside the project, with crane, transport, and storage, and its own budget and contingency; it is often the first proper look at the mast step and chainplates.

Berths. Pricing is by length overall, so sailing and motor yachts of the same length pay roughly the same. A handful of marinas (Antibes, Saint Tropez, Newport, Saint Maarten) hold preferred slots for significant sailing yachts during regatta windows.

Total operating cost. A 50m sailing yacht at moderate use typically runs 70 to 85 percent of the equivalent motor figure. The differential narrows in the 24 to 40m band and widens above 60m where motor fuel and crew cost grow disproportionately.

paragraphs.text: We have the mainsail reefed and the J4 out. We’re surfing waves doing 20 knots, dolphins jumping out around us. There’s a thrill in that which you would never get on a motorboat.
paragraphs.attribution: Capt. Ella Johnson, sailing yacht captain, May 2026

paragraphs.text: Carbon and regulation

paragraphs: Three regulatory and market shifts have changed the carbon conversation since 2020.

EU ETS Maritime is the best known, and it reaches fewer yachts than is often assumed. In force from 1 January 2024, it applies to ships of 5,000 GT and above that carry passengers or cargo for commercial purposes to or from EEA ports. Compliance is phased by emissions year: 40 percent of 2024 emissions (surrendered in 2025), 70 percent of 2025 emissions, and 100 percent of 2026 emissions onward, first due by 30 September 2027. A yacht in private use sits outside the system at any size. A yacht of 5,000 GT or more on commercial charter can fall inside it, and published guidance does not settle the position of charter yachts certified for 12 passengers or fewer. Very few yachts reach the threshold in any case (a 60m motor yacht is typically 700 to 1,200 GT). In July 2026 the European Commission proposed extending the system to selected ship types between 400 and 5,000 GT from 2031; the proposal does not name yachts, and negotiation runs into 2027.

The addition of methane and nitrous oxide to the system from 2026 matters most for liquefied natural gas (LNG)-fuelled vessels where methane slip is significant. For diesel-fuelled engines and diesel hotel-load generators on most yachts, methane emissions are negligible; the practical taxation effect remains on CO2.

The IMO 2023 Strategy (MEPC 80, Resolution MEPC.377(80)) sets a 20 percent well-to-wake GHG reduction by 2030 (striving 30), 70 percent by 2040 (striving 80), net zero by or around 2050, against 2008 levels. The strategy shapes the commercial shipping fuel transition that reaches yachting through fuel availability and cost. The IMO Net-Zero Framework, which would add a global fuel standard and emissions pricing for ships of 5,000 GT and above in international shipping, was approved in April 2025; a vote to adopt it was adjourned in October 2025 and resumes on 4 December 2026. If adopted it could not enter into force before 2028, and whether it would reach yachts is not settled. Closer to hand are the IMO emission control areas. The Mediterranean has required 0.10 percent sulphur fuel since May 2025. A new North-East Atlantic area, covering the waters of the United Kingdom, Ireland and Atlantic France, Spain and Portugal, enters into force on 1 September 2027, with low-sulphur fuel required there from September 2028 and NOx Tier III engines for ships constructed from 1 January 2027, a date set by contract, keel-laying or delivery. A buyer contracting a new build in 2027 for Atlantic Europe should confirm with class how Tier III applies.

The nearest practical answer is hydrotreated vegetable oil. HVO is a paraffinic diesel made from waste fats and vegetable oils and a drop-in replacement for marine gas oil: engines approved for paraffinic fuel run on it, usually without change to fuel systems or tanks, and the engine maker’s approval should be confirmed. Made from waste feedstocks, its lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions are up to about 90 percent below fossil diesel, depending on the feedstock and the accounting rules used. The CO2 from the exhaust is much the same as diesel’s; the saving lies in where the carbon came from. A cetane number above 70 gives cleaner combustion. Bunker availability is strongest in the Mediterranean, weaker in the Caribbean and US East Coast, mixed elsewhere; it is priced at a premium over mineral diesel that varies widely by port and supplier. Feadship’s 84m Obsidian, delivered in 2023, was designed and sea-trialled to run on HVO; uptake among other quality builders has accelerated. For owners wanting a defensible carbon position without rebuilding the engine room, HVO is the easiest move available.

Methanol and hydrogen-fuel-cell drives are moving from concept to delivery; both require significant new-build engineering. Methanol-ready arrangements are appearing in the larger Northern European order books, and fuel cells are already in delivered hulls for hotel load and low-speed running: Sanlorenzo delivered a 50 metre yacht with a methanol reformer fuel cell in 2024, Feadship’s 118.8 metre Breakthrough carries hydrogen fuel cells, and Lürssen launched a 114 metre methanol fuel-cell yacht in 2025 and delivered her in 2026. For most readers, HVO and hybrid drive are the practical near-term options.

Capgemini’s 2024 World Wealth Report identifies sustainability as a major concern for next-generation HNWIs. A yacht is conspicuous in a way a family office’s liquid portfolio is not, and a growing number of principals want the carbon question answered in advance. On the fuel figures above, a 50m sailing yacht emits about two thirds less CO2 a year than the comparable motor yacht. At about 2.75 kg of CO2 per litre of marine diesel burned (the IMO factor of 3.206 tonnes of CO2 per tonne of fuel), the motor yacht’s 110,000 to 270,000 litres give roughly 300 to 740 tonnes a year and the sailing yacht’s 33,000 to 92,000 litres roughly 90 to 250 tonnes. The comparison covers fuel burned aboard only. It leaves out the production of the fuel, the build, refits, sails and travel to and from the yacht, and it assumes the sailing yacht is sailed rather than motored.

paragraphs.text: Hybrid and electric drive, the third path

paragraphs: Hybrid propulsion has moved from concept to delivery and changes the motor-versus-sail decision. Two builders are the published reference points.

Heesen Yachts’ hybrid programme is the deepest commercial deployment of parallel diesel-electric propulsion in production yachts. The 50 metre FDHF aluminium series (Home, Amare II, Project Orion early 2025) pairs two main diesels, two diesel generators, and two electric motors operable separately or in combination. Owners use electric for harbour transits, anchor approaches, and short coastal hops; diesels for passage. Owners report meaningful annual fuel reductions; the operational character is closer to a sailing yacht’s silence at anchor than to conventional motor.

Royal Huisman has taken the deeper-engineering route. Aquarius II, a 65 metre sailing yacht delivered in 2025, integrates semi-hybrid power generation with battery and load smoothing, supported by hydro-generators that trickle-charge under sail. The shipyard’s AERA concept (with Rondal, Artemis Technologies, Cor D. Rover Design) layers wind-assisted propulsion, hydro-generation, and a hydrogen fuel cell for up to 72 hours of zero-emission operation at anchor, with a 580 kWh battery bank sized to run hotel load silently for around 11 hours. AERA remains a concept; the underlying technologies are in delivered hulls.

At the wind-and-solar end sits Captain Arctic, a 70 metre polar expedition ship for 36 passengers built in Mauritius for the French operator Selar, with solar-panelled rigid sails and electric propulsion that doubles as hydro-generation under sail. She is a passenger ship rather than a yacht, but she shows how far the technology behind concepts such as AERA has reached (Gayle Patterson, Pelorus Yachting, in The Superyacht Report, Q2 2026).

For the buyer thinking about the next ten years, hybrid and electric capability is now a question to ask of any new build, sailing or motor. Bering Yachts, Wider, Sanlorenzo (SX series), Lürssen, Feadship, and Oceanco all have hybrid hulls in build or delivered. The decision now has three options, with hybrid between the other two.

BoatPro’s 2026 order-book engine breakdown shows the scale. Diesel remains overwhelmingly the dominant propulsion among in-build hulls, hybrid orders are rising sharply year-on-year off a small base, diesel-electric is in a similar trajectory, and pure electric is flat at a handful of units. The direction is clear; the share is still small. A new-build buyer asking the hybrid question in 2027 is still asking it earlier than most of the order book, not late.

A fourth pattern is the multihull. Catamarans are the only sub-segment of the sailing market reporting unit growth among UHNW buyers (Fraser Yachts, May 2026). Baltic Yachts has a catamaran in build for 2027 delivery; the yard frames the multihull as the first stage of crossover between motor and sail, offering the flat platform a motor-side buyer expects on a yacht that runs primarily under sail. The category is too small to characterise residual behaviour reliably, and the argument that the multihull is the natural compromise between the two rests on early evidence. The refit side differs too. A large catamaran can exceed the lift beam of yards that are otherwise ideal, and the bridgedeck, bulkhead bonding, and load paths need a surveyor who knows where to look (Refit Advisory Group).

A fifth, separate from the propulsion debate, is the explorer: SeaXplorer, Damen Yacht Support, and the high-latitude end of the Northern European order book, where the cost shape is determined by self-sufficiency rather than hospitality.

paragraphs.text: Racing pedigree and value retention

paragraphs: At the top of the sailing market, racing pedigree is among the strongest supports of residual value. Three circuits matter.

The J Class. Nine hulls active: three surviving originals (Velsheda, Shamrock, Endeavour) refitted for cruising and racing, plus six modern builds since 2003 (Ranger, Rainbow, Hanuman, Lionheart, Topaz, Svea). They race at Newport, Saint Barths Bucket, Maxi Yacht Rolex Cup, J Class World Championship. A further hull is reported in build at Brodotrogir, Croatia. Provenance, regatta access, and the closed class support residuals well above comparable cruising sailing yachts; a hold-forever asset for the families who own them.

The Maxi and Wally circuit. Maxi Yacht Rolex Cup (Porto Cervo), Voiles de Saint Tropez, Loro Piana Superyacht Regatta, Antigua Bermuda Race form the Maxi season. Wally hulls (Wally B, Wallygator, Wally 80 to 130) trade actively with strong residuals at the top.

The RORC calendar. Fastnet, RORC Caribbean 600, Middle Sea Race, Transatlantic Race. Offshore-capable yachts (typically 18 to 30m) for which a racing record can support resale value against a comparable cruising hull, though no published sales data put a figure on the premium.

Two 2025 reference points illustrate segment health. Edmiston and Nautor Swan announced an alloy sailing yacht range at the 2025 Palm Beach International Boat Show, designed by Malcolm McKeon Yacht Design. Tom Cruise was reported in 2025 to have ordered a Swan 108, a 33m carbon-fibre racing-capable sailing yacht at Nautor Swan, Jakobstad, estimated above USD 30 million. Committed capital and leading design houses are building modern sailing yachts at the top of the market.

By May 2026, Palma International Boat Show added further evidence of segment differentiation. Will Bishop of Superyacht Partners describes the performance sailing yacht market between 28 and 34 metres as trading strongly, often off-market, while the 35 to 45 metre band sits noticeably softer (Superyacht Investor, May 2026). Baltic Yachts presented Canova (43m, asking EUR 29.8 million, the owner’s fifth Baltic yacht). Southern Wind delivered SW108 Kalantis in February 2026 against an August 2024 contract; the yard reports its next available build slot is in 2028, the new owner is in his 30s, and the average ownership age across the three Southern Wind hulls at Palma sits in the late 40s. The age curve at the buyer end of the sailing yacht market is moving down.
Georges Bourgoignie of Fraser added the broker-side counterweight on the same coverage:

paragraphs.text: It’s so much more work to sell a sailboat, but it’s somehow more fulfilling. But it’s tough and getting tougher.
paragraphs.attribution: Georges Bourgoignie, Fraser, Palma May 2026 (Superyacht Investor)

paragraphs: Broker commentary describes the sailing segment as healthier than the headline unit-share suggests, and harder to transact; both can be true.
Stefan Zimmermann Zschocke, CEO of Oyster Yachts, on the Superyacht Investor London panel in April 2026, located the buyer-side instinct behind the sail demand at the top of the segment:

paragraphs.text: We’re seeing more and more younger centi-millionaires coming. So these centi-millionaires, at least in our niche, they want to have a purpose … either authenticity, adventure or community.
paragraphs.attribution: Stefan Zimmermann Zschocke, CEO, Oyster Yachts (Superyacht Investor London, April 2026)

paragraphs: The Oyster World Rally, the owner-driven circumnavigation Oyster runs roughly every other year, is the operational expression of the purpose Zimmermann Zschocke describes: authenticity, adventure or community. The retention thesis the segment uses sits on top of it: the buyer who completes one rally tends to commission the next, larger boat.

paragraphs.text: Seven-year cost on a 35 metre

paragraphs: For a buyer in the 24 to 40 metre band, a sailing yacht typically costs less to build and to run than a motor yacht of comparable build quality, so each week aboard costs less.

A new build 35m sailing yacht from a quality builder (Pendennis, Vitters, Baltic) runs EUR 12 to 22 million; a comparable 35m motor yacht runs EUR 18 to 30 million. The sailing yacht typically costs 20 to 35 percent less to build. Annual operating cost runs 70 to 85 percent of the motor figure. Most of that cost is fixed whatever the use (chapter 1), so the saving does not of itself buy more weeks aboard. It lowers the cost of each week: a motor yacht with a EUR 1.5 million budget used for 12 weeks costs about EUR 125,000 a week, and a sailing yacht at the same use costs EUR 1.05 to 1.28 million a year, or about EUR 88,000 to 106,000 a week.

Depreciation. Broker-aggregated data suggests that quality sailing yachts in the 30 to 50m band hold value better than comparable motor yachts. Chapter 1 gives the general curve: about 30 to 43 percent lost by year five, with the best builders on both sides (Feadship, Lürssen, Royal Huisman, Vitters, Baltic) losing single-digit percentages a year after that. Across a seven-year hold, on the capital and operating figures above, a 35m sailing programme runs about a fifth to a third below the equivalent motor on total cost (capex plus opex minus residual) if both lose value at the same rate, and 25 to 40 percent below if the sailing yacht keeps about ten percentage points more of its value.

paragraphs.text: Where the case for sail does not hold

paragraphs: There are owners for whom a sailing yacht is the wrong answer, and the cases are worth naming.

Sailing yachts ask more from the operation: sail-handling expertise on the deck team, careful weather routing, and itineraries that bend to the wind. An owner who needs to cross the Atlantic on a fixed schedule with no flexibility on the weather window is not a sailing-yacht owner. An owner comfortable with a 36 to 60 hour weather window for a transatlantic is.

Sailing yachts are heavier on the body and on time. A motor yacht delivers a steady ride at displacement speed. A sailing yacht heels, accelerates, decelerates, and asks more of the people aboard. Older owners, owners with mobility constraints, and owners who use the yacht primarily for entertaining rather than cruising are often better served by a motor yacht (or a hybrid one).

The supply side is thinner. There are fewer high-quality sailing yacht builders, fewer slot opportunities, and a smaller pool of comparable hulls in the brokerage market. A buyer who wants a 35 metre sailing yacht in 2027 has a shorter list of credible options than a buyer looking for a 35 metre motor yacht.

paragraphs.text: Three threshold tests

paragraphs: Three questions tend to decide it for any specific buyer.

First, what does the cruising calendar look like? An owner whose programme depends on fixed-date passages with no weather contingency is on the motor or hybrid side. An owner with a season of cruising flexibility is on the sailing-yacht side, or has a real choice across all three.

Second, how exposed is the buyer to the carbon question? A principal whose family office, foundation, or public profile pulls at the carbon line will sit closer to the sailing yacht or hybrid side. A principal for whom carbon is not a board-level conversation will weight the cruising-calendar question more heavily.

Third, what is the seven-year arithmetic? Run capex, opex, depreciation, and residual against the buyer’s actual use case before defaulting either way. Many first-time buyers default to motor without doing the comparison; some of them are right to, others are not.

09-decision-framework.title: The decision framework
09-decision-framework.standfirst: The ownership structure that comes first. The team that protects you, in the order that matters. The independence test, applied transparently to every adviser including us.
paragraphs: The UBS Global Family Office Report 2025 is among the most comprehensive surveys of how the world’s largest private wealth holders allocate capital. Across 80 pages and 317 family offices (average AUM USD 1.1 billion, average family net worth USD 2.7 billion), yachts do not appear in any region or sub-allocation, and the 2026 edition, covering 307 family offices, does not mention them either. The survey does not show what individual family offices hold, but it does show that yachts sit outside the allocation framework the industry uses to describe family-office wealth.

Many of the buyers described in chapter 2, principals who have recently sold a business and heirs reviewing the advisers their parents used, reach this market through a family office. The Knight Frank Family Office Survey 2026, drawn from more than 40 family offices in London, New York, Dubai, Singapore and Hong Kong, names superyachts for the first time, among the assets family offices now want to track in one place:

paragraphs.text: Digital aggregation, enabling live, consolidated tracking of complex portfolios, from liquid assets to superyachts and real estate.
paragraphs.attribution: Knight Frank Family Office Survey 2026

paragraphs: Family offices are working to bring yachts into the same reporting as their other assets, although the tooling is still being built. Better tooling will not show how the advisers around a purchase are paid; chapter 3 sets that out. What the buyer can do is settle the structure first, test every adviser, and hire the team in the right order.

paragraphs.text: The structure comes first

paragraphs: Before testing any adviser, the reader has to understand what is being built. The ownership structure is the vehicle that holds the yacht: personal ownership, a company, or something more layered, together with the jurisdiction it occupies and the VAT position that rides on it. It is among the first decisions an owner makes, among the hardest to unwind, and the one most often left too late; settling it early, and around the owner rather than the transaction’s timetable, is among the first things an independent adviser is engaged to ensure. We put it to Simon Roberts of Quadrant Group, which has built these structures from the Isle of Man for forty years; his answers, on jurisdiction, VAT, private against commercial use, the annual cost, and the decision hardest to reverse, are in the interview that closes this chapter.

paragraphs.text: The structure should be built around the owner’s objectives, rather than the other way around.
paragraphs.attribution: Simon Roberts, Quadrant Group

paragraphs: A yacht is rarely the principal’s only significant asset, and its ownership structure should not be designed as though it were. The vehicle that holds the yacht sits alongside the family’s operating companies, property, trusts, and succession arrangements, and the sound version of the decision reads across all of them at once. Residency and tax position are shared inputs; a jurisdiction that suits the yacht in isolation can work against the structure the family already runs elsewhere, or complicate the estate the next generation inherits.

The yacht is therefore planned with the principal’s wider wealth, as the family-office material above suggests, not bolted on beside it. The jurisdiction is chosen last, once those wider circumstances are known, which is why there is no single right answer to carry from one owner to the next.

paragraphs.text: For first-time owners, the key is not to ask, “Which jurisdiction is best?” but rather, “Which jurisdiction is best for my circumstances?”
paragraphs.attribution: Simon Roberts, Quadrant Group

paragraphs.text: Two developments in 2026 bear on how the holding structure is built. On 21 May 2026 the Court of Justice of the European Union held, in joined Cases C-428/24 and C-476/24 concerning Sailing Yacht A, that assets held in a trust can be treated under EU sanctions law as owned or controlled by a sanctioned beneficiary, and that terms in the trust deed do not of themselves prevent a freeze. The case has returned to the Italian courts and the yacht remains seized. A trust above the yacht’s holding company is a succession arrangement; it does not place the yacht beyond measures aimed at the person who benefits from it. Separately, Switzerland opened a federal register of beneficial owners on 1 October 2026. It is not public, but a Swiss company, or a foreign holding company whose decisions are in practice taken in Switzerland, must file the natural persons who control it, with changes reported within a month. From the same date, Swiss lawyers, fiduciaries and multi-family offices that set up or fund a company abroad for a client carry anti-money-laundering due diligence, including questions on the source of funds where the risk warrants it.
The independence test

paragraphs: The independence test has six elements, and chapter 3 explains why it is needed. It applies to any adviser, including the publisher of The First Owner’s Reference; the publisher’s own answers are on the colophon.

1. Does the firm earn anything contingent on a transaction closing, and if so, has it disclosed in writing what it is paid and by whom? Brokers, charter brokers, management companies that receive yard referral fees, and design firms taking commission on builder selection all earn in this way. That does not rule them out. Disclosed in advance and in writing, the payment is something the buyer can weigh against the advice; undisclosed, it fails this element.

2. Does the firm hold any equity, employment, or referral relationship with any yard, broker, supplier, management company, or charter operation? If yes, they are not independent of those counterparties. A management company owned by a brokerage is not independent of that brokerage’s recommendations.

3. Does the firm publish a complete counterparty list for the past three years, with the nature of each relationship? If no, the reader cannot test claims one and two; the independence claim becomes assertion rather than evidence.

4. Are the firm’s fees transparent and quoted in writing in advance? If no, the fee arrangement can hide commissions. Hourly without a cap, or percentage without a clear scope, has the latitude to extract value the buyer cannot price.

5. Does the firm hold professional indemnity insurance at a level appropriate to the transaction? If no, the firm cannot afford to be wrong on the buyer’s behalf. A USD 50 million build with an adviser carrying GBP 1 million PI is not insured against the actual scale.

6. Are the firm’s principals named, traceable, and accountable? If no, none of the above can be verified. Anonymous firms, firms registered in jurisdictions without beneficial-ownership disclosure, firms whose principals do not appear in public communications, fail the most basic accountability test.

The same six questions serve as a first check on a wealth manager, a lawyer, a surveyor or a captain candidate. They are ordinary fiduciary principles, not yacht-specific ones, applied to a market in which much of the advice is paid for by someone other than the buyer.

paragraphs.text: The suitability test

paragraphs: This is a separate test from the independence test. Where the independence test asks whose interests a firm serves, the suitability test asks whether it is the right firm for this engagement. A firm can pass the independence test and still be the wrong choice for a given project. The suitability test also has six elements.

1. Comparable track record. Has the firm delivered projects in the same size band, the same yard tier, and the same regime (new build, refit, brokerage acquisition; sail or motor; semi-custom or fully custom) as the engagement in question? A firm with deep refit experience on 50 metre motor yachts is not, by default, the right firm for a 70 metre custom sailing yacht new build. Ask for three named examples in the comparable band.

2. Team breadth against the project’s actual needs. Does the firm carry, in-house or in retained relationships, the specialist disciplines the project will require: maritime counsel introduction, paint surveying, vibration and acoustic engineering, mechanical and propulsion review, electrical compliance, refund-guarantee credit assessment, and post-delivery warranty management? A representative who has to subcontract every specialism is more expensive and slower than one who carries the disciplines.

3. Bandwidth. How many concurrent projects is the firm running, how many will the named principals personally lead, and what proportion of the work passes to junior staff? Ask for the principal’s expected on-site days per month and the project manager’s expected on-site days per week, in writing.

4. Geographic presence. Where is the firm based relative to the yard, the surveyor’s likely ports, and the owner’s preferred operating area? A representative based two flights from the yard, on a build that demands weekly site presence, will either spend the budget on travel or miss the site visits the build needs. Ask about office or partner presence in the relevant geographies.

5. Willingness to decline. Has the firm walked away from engagements where the right advice was for the client not to proceed, or where the proposed structure failed independence or suitability review? A firm that cannot point to engagements declined or terminated has not been tested. The willingness to walk is the clearest evidence of whose interest a firm serves.

6. Reference depth. Will the firm provide named references, including at least one engagement that did not land cleanly? The reference list of triumphs is universal. The reference list that includes a project where things ran hot, and what the firm did about it, is the test. A firm that cannot produce one has either not been busy long enough, or has not been honest about what busy means.

A representative who answers these six questions clearly, with documentary evidence, is suited to the engagement they are being considered for. A representative who cannot is not necessarily a poor firm; they may be the right firm for a different project.

The independence test and the suitability test are applied together. A firm that passes both is the firm to engage. A separate filter is the Yacht Owner’s Representative Register, the cross-industry register of vetted representatives administered by the Superyacht Alliance for Professional Standards. The publisher of The First Owner’s Reference offers both tests for application to itself alongside any other firm a reader is considering.

paragraphs.text: Building the team, in priority order

paragraphs: The order in which the buyer hires the team shapes every later decision, because each adviser hired early has a say in who is hired next. A buyer who starts with a broker will often be introduced to the lawyer, the surveyor and the captain by that broker, as chapter 3 describes. The order this book recommends:

1. Independent adviser (the owner’s representative, on a new build or refit; chapter 3 defines the role). Engaged before any broker, any captain, any management company. The adviser’s role is to scope the acquisition, evaluate brokers, support the negotiation, and build the rest of the team.

2. Yacht lawyer and structuring adviser. Specialist shipbuilding and yacht counsel from a recognised firm (Hill Dickinson, Watson Farley & Williams, Ince, Stephenson Harwood, Reed Smith, HFW, Norton Rose Fulbright). Engaged before any contract is reviewed. The ownership structure, jurisdiction and VAT position are settled at this stage, with the corporate services provider or tax adviser who will run the structure, as set out above. The independent adviser will introduce candidates and disclose any relationship with them.

On a new build, the security position between signature and delivery has no natural owner. Lawyers are engaged to negotiate the contract and released once it is signed; brokers are paid at signature; surveyors attend milestones only where someone has instructed them. Jack MacNally of Foreland Marine, the publisher of this reference, made the point in The Superyacht Report (issue 230, September 2026): below roughly 500 GT and EUR 30 million, responsibility for the file, in the banking sense, sits with no one. The buyer assigns that responsibility, in writing, to one member of the team.

3. Surveyor. Engaged on a per-deal basis once a shortlist exists. Independent of the broker. Recognised firms include Ward & McKenzie and Patton Marine. The surveyor’s report is paid for by the buyer.

4. Captain candidate (or build captain on new build). Hired through routes independent of the broker. Interviewed at length. The captain should be involved in survey, sea trial, and acceptance decisions.
5. Yacht management company. Engaged once the acquisition decision is taken. Independent of the broker. The management company is the long-running operational partner.

6. Insurance broker. Engaged once flag state and operating profile are determined. Insurance brokers are usually paid by commission embedded in the premium; the rate, and any referral fee paid onward, should be disclosed in writing, which meets the first element of the independence test. Obtain at least three quotes; chapter 7 names the main brokers.
Total team cost on a USD 30 to 50 million acquisition runs USD 200,000 to 600,000 across the first year, between about 0.4 and 2 percent of the price.

paragraphs.text: The ten questions

paragraphs: A one-page checklist the reader can apply before signing anything.
1. Who introduced the yacht (or yard) to me, and who pays them?
2. Who recommended the lawyer, and who pays them?
3. Who recommended the surveyor, and who pays them?
4. Who recommended the management company, and who pays them?
5. Has any party offered to provide their services “at no cost,” and if so, who is paying them?
6. Has every party I am working with disclosed their commercial relationships in writing, including referral fees, retrocessions, and equity holdings in counterparties?
7. Is my legal counsel independent of the broker, the yard, and the management company, and is their fee paid by me directly?
8. Is my surveyor independent of the seller and of the broker, and is their fee paid by me directly?
9. If I am building, is my owner’s representative paid by me, and has any contingent fee, yard commission or referral relationship been disclosed to me in writing?
10. If I asked any of these parties to walk away from a deal that would not benefit me, would they?
A buyer who can answer all ten clearly, with documents to show for it, is well protected. A question the buyer cannot answer is the next one to put, in writing, to the party concerned.

paragraphs.text: The ten questions, the hiring order, and the independence test are collected on a single reference page for use during a live transaction.

closingNote: The First Owner’s Reference exists because trade press is structurally less able to publish what is set out across these chapters. None of this is a moral failing of the people who work in trade press; it is a fact about how the industry funds itself. The publisher of this reference is funded by independent consultancy work rather than advertising, and that single difference is more or less the entire publication. The publisher’s own answers to the independence test are on the colophon.

For a reader considering a first acquisition, whether as a principal who has recently sold a business or as an heir for whom the family yacht has become a new responsibility, the months before the first contract matter most. The ownership structure, the team and the order in which it is hired are settled in that window, and each is harder and more costly to change once a contract is signed.
The single most important decision is to engage an adviser who works for the buyer and is paid by the buyer, before engaging anyone paid by someone else. That is the argument. The rest is detail.
There are several such advisers. The publisher of The First Owner’s Reference is one of them. The independence test, applied to all of them, is how the right one is chosen.
